title: URL-Sim: Unified and Regulated LiDAR Simulation for High-Fidelity Reconstruction of Dynamic Driving Scenes
summary: Reconstructing high-fidelity LiDAR simulation scenes from real-world driving logs is essential for cost-effective safety validation of autonomous driving systems. While simulators based on Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) achieve realistic scene reconstruction, their large-scale adoption is limited by slow rendering speeds. Recent 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) approaches have improved rendering efficiency through explicit primitive representation and differentiable rasterization. However, existing 3DGS-based methods remain largely restricted to rigid vehicles and produce redundant primitives through unconstrained densification. To address these limitations, we propose URL-Sim, a unified and regulated dynamic LiDAR simulation framework. URL-Sim constructs a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that decouples the modeling of traffic participants, including vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists, enabling accurate reconstruction of heterogeneous dynamic objects within a single framework. It further introduces a regulated Gaussian densification strategy that ranks primitives with multi-dimensional importance scores and allocates Gaussians to the most critical regions while keeping the total primitive count bounded. Experiments on the Waymo and KITTI-360 datasets demonstrate that URL-Sim achieves higher quantitative accuracy and visual quality than existing baselines under comparable primitive budgets, and accurately recovers the geometry and poses of diverse dynamic traffic participants.

LiDAR simulation, Gaussian splatting, dynamic scene graph, non-rigid modeling, autonomous driving. Introduction iDAR sensors are integral to environmental perception in advanced autonomous driving systems 1 , making the driving-scene data they provide critical for the testing and validation of perception and planning algorithms 2 . Since traditional on-road data collection is inefficient and offers limited scene coverage, there is an increasing need for efficient and realistic LiDAR simulation methods 3 . Traditional LiDAR simulation, whether physics-engine-based virtual worlds CARLA,AirSim,6 or explicit geometric reconstruction LiDARsim,8,9,PCGen , suffers from substantial sim-to-real gaps, cumbersome pipelines, and limited support for dynamic scenes. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) nerf narrow the sim-to-real gap for LiDAR simulation using continuous implicit representations and differentiable volume rendering NFL,LiDAR-NeRF,UniSim,NeuRAD . Some methods incorporate spatio-temporal constraints LiDAR4D and bounding box tracking DyNFL to handle dynamic scenes. However, the dense ray sampling inherent in volume rendering causes substantial computational overhead. The consequent slow training and rendering speeds cannot meet the requirements of large-scale modeling and real-time closed-loop simulation. Recent 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) 3dgs has emerged as an effective alternative to NeRF, achieving order-of-magnitude improvements in rendering efficiency through its explicit Gaussian representation and hardware-accelerated rendering. While current mainstream methods 4dgs,drivinggs,omnire,streetgs primarily focus on camera data synthesis, seminal works such as GS-LiDAR gslidar and LiDAR-GS lidargs have successfully adapted 3DGS to the LiDAR imaging model by designing differentiable splatting pipelines tailored to LiDAR's active perception mechanism. To handle dynamic scenes, LiDAR-RT LiDAR-RT and SplatAD SplatAD employ a dynamic-static separation strategy to model rigid vehicles separately. Despite these advances, existing Gaussian-based LiDAR simulation methods face two primary challenges. First, current dynamic scene simulations primarily focus on rigid objects and provide limited support for non-rigid entities such as pedestrians and cyclists, who are vulnerable road users central to high-risk edge cases. Second, existing methods incur substantial computational overhead, driven by the inherent sparsity and non-uniform angular distribution of LiDAR point clouds, combined with the unrestricted densification of the Gaussian paradigm. These issues reduce training efficiency and simulation performance, potentially triggering training failures and constraining practical scalability and scene adaptability. To address these challenges, URL-Sim is proposed as a unified and regulated LiDAR simulation framework for the high-fidelity reconstruction and controllable editing of dynamic urban driving scenes. URL-Sim constructs a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that decouples individual dynamic entities from the static background for independent modeling. Rigid objects such as vehicles are simulated via standard rigid transformations. For non-rigid entities such as pedestrians, the Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) smpl model is introduced to serve as a deformation prior. Specifically, the Gaussian primitives of each pedestrian are bound to the SMPL mesh vertices, and the pose and shape parameters of the model are utilized to drive the skinning deformation of the Gaussians. For template-free non-rigid objects such as cyclists, a lightweight deformation network is employed to directly learn and optimize the local deformation parameters. Together, these three representations enable unified modeling and simulation of the principal traffic participants in autonomous driving. To curb the unconstrained expansion of primitives and the redundant accumulation of Gaussians inherent in the original Adaptive Density Control (ADC), a regulated Gaussian densification (RGD) strategy is proposed. RGD imposes a predefined global upper bound on the total Gaussian count and allocates a fixed budget for each densification step following a quadratic growth curve, establishing a deterministic training schedule. A Gaussian importance scoring system is constructed by integrating spatial gradients, image-domain features, and rendering accumulation attributes. Guided by these scores, targeted densification and adaptive pruning are executed within the allocated single-round budget. This controllable mechanism limits redundant proliferation and achieves higher rendering performance under a strictly bounded primitive count. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: URL-Sim is presented as a unified and regulated LiDAR simulation framework that models diverse dynamic non-rigid objects, addressing a relatively under-explored problem in LiDAR simulation. A regulated Gaussian densification strategy is proposed to balance simulation accuracy and computational overhead through quadratic budget allocation and multi-dimensional scoring. Extensive experiments on Waymo and KITTI-360 validate accurate recovery of non-rigid actor geometry and poses, as well as competitive 2D perceptual quality and 3D geometric accuracy. Related work LiDAR Simulation and Novel View Synthesis Classical LiDAR simulation relies on virtual platforms such as CARLA CARLA and AirSim AirSim for environmental control and closed-loop interaction 6 , but inherently suffers from severe sim-to-real domain gaps. Efforts to bridge this gap through physical modeling LiDARsim and real-world asset libraries 8,9 are hindered by cumbersome procedures and high labor costs. Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) nerf have advanced LiDAR simulation through implicit spatial modeling and volume rendering, narrowing the sim-to-real gap. Early frameworks including NFL NFL and LiDAR-NeRF LiDAR-NeRF integrate the LiDAR imaging process into NeRF to enable high-quality novel view synthesis. For complex dynamic scenes, UniSim UniSim and NeuRAD NeuRAD utilize feature grids and precise physical modeling to reconstruct and recompose traffic participants. DyNFL DyNFL and LiDAR4D LiDAR4D further isolate dynamic objects and capture temporal correlations to achieve editable digital twins and high-fidelity 4D spatio-temporal synthesis. Nevertheless, the reliance on high-frequency dense sampling induces considerable computational overhead and slow rendering speeds, precluding real-time closed-loop deployment. 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) 3dgs offers a real-time alternative via its explicit primitive representation and highly parallelized rasterization. Early 3DGS-based methods such as GS-LiDAR gslidar and LiDAR-GS lidargs render substantially faster than NeRF-based counterparts with comparable reconstruction quality, but are limited to static scenes and lack editability. LiDAR-RT LiDAR-RT separates dynamic and static components using bounding boxes and tracking IDs to enable customizable scene editing. SplatAD SplatAD and SIMULI SimULi similarly rely on 3DGS for joint camera-LiDAR simulation. However, these approaches are predominantly restricted to rigid vehicles and overlook non-rigid objects such as pedestrians and cyclists. Moreover, current frameworks lack resource-efficient mechanisms for controlling redundant Gaussians resulting from unconstrained densification. Gaussian Resource Optimization Although 3DGS demonstrates promising sensor simulation capabilities, its heuristic cloning and splitting generate redundant Gaussian primitives, inflating VRAM consumption and storage steepest,apn . Various approaches have been proposed to optimize the computational efficiency of 3DGS for large-scale deployment. The first category targets post-processing of redundant models via compression and pruning. Compact 3DGS compact3dgs and Compressed 3DGS compressed3dgs employ vector quantization and entropy coding to compress Gaussian parameters, reducing storage without altering underlying spatial geometry. Pruning strategies eliminate Gaussian primitives with marginal visual contributions, guided by metrics such as multi-view consistency, uncertainty scores, and global importance reducing,pup,lightgaussian . Although model volume is substantially reduced, excessive pruning at extreme compression ratios frequently leads to severe visual degradation and loss of foreground geometric details. The second category optimizes densification during training to prevent redundant generation at its source, replacing unconstrained growth with rigorous control. SteepGS steepest and Taming 3DGS taming minimize redundant sub-Gaussians through analytical optimization and fixed-budget constructive pipelines. BUGS bus employs a region-consistency-based bi-directional growing mechanism to adaptively regulate Gaussian density for compact scene reconstruction. For LiDAR geometry, GTLR-GS gtlr and GeomGS geomgs incorporate curvature-adaptive refinement and geometric confidence scores to govern densification. These works demonstrate that proactive densification is critical for compact, high-fidelity reconstruction. Nevertheless, these strategies are designed for visual modalities and rely on dense pixel-level observations. When applied directly to LiDAR simulation, they may misallocate Gaussian primitives by overlooking sparse ray-level geometry and intensity cues, thereby compromising range accuracy and foreground structural fidelity. Given raw LiDAR point clouds and object bounding boxes, URL-Sim builds a dynamic Gaussian scene graph that models the static background and dynamic instances separately. Each instance is transformed to world coordinates at its timestamp and composed with the background. title: RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement
summary: Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

Improving execution alone leaves this choice unchanged. Useful practice changes as an agent's capabilities develop. A drawer skill that succeeds alone can still fail when composed with object placement, so practice must probe the composition as well as its individual steps. Selecting such practice requires interpreting prior outcomes, identifying prerequisites, and retaining conditions that reveal regressions. Automatic curricula already connect practice selection with skill accumulation wang2023voyager , but the selection procedure itself must also adapt as failures are resolved and new interactions emerge. Earlier rules for finding informative challenges can then become inadequate. This motivates a robot self-improvement loop that revises how it chooses practice alongside how it executes tasks. We introduce (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), in which a curriculum harness and an execution harness evolve through an adversarial interaction (Figure~ fig:practice-partners ). A harness contains the prompts, skills, tools, interfaces, and agent-readable memory that organize behavior around frozen foundation models. The curriculum side uses prior capability evidence to expose weaknesses in the current execution harness. summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models now exceed 95% success on the LIBERO simulation benchmark, yet it remains unclear how much of this performance requires generalization beyond the training demonstrations. In this work, we show that retrieving nearby demonstrations and reusing their action chunks achieves a success rate of 91.7 % on LIBERO without policy training. Under LIBERO-Plus perturbations, retrieval shows the smallest drop of all evaluated policies. Across nine publicly available VLAs, fine-tuning mostly makes the vision-language backbone a better retrieval key, and the actions of the VLAs remain close to the demonstrations. In addition, we introduce Local Action Consistency (LAC), an offline metric that measures whether nearby observations in representation space are also associated with similar future actions. We show that LAC tracks the success rate of retrieval and can guide the training of a retrieval key. Our evaluation and source code are available at https://github.com/sereact/lerobot_knn.

Introduction sec:introduction Modern models typically combine a large pretrained vision-language backbone with an action-generation head (e.g., regression, diffusion, or flow matching). These models are further pretrained on large, heterogeneous collections of robot trajectories and subsequently fine-tuned for downstream manipulation tasks~ pi2025pi05 . Their performance is commonly evaluated on standardized benchmarks, which measure closed-loop task success across predefined tasks and initial conditions. Among these, the ~ liu2023libero is one of the most widely used simulation benchmarks, consisting of language-conditioned Franka manipulation tasks across five suites: LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, with tasks each, and LIBERO-90 and LIBERO-Long, with and tasks, respectively. Each task comes with demonstrations. are commonly fine-tuned on these demonstrations and evaluated in closed loop from a fixed set of benchmark initial states. Recent progress has pushed LIBERO close to saturation, with several modern reporting success rates around or above ~ Kim2025,pi2025pi05,sun2026vlajepa , making further gains increasingly difficult to interpret as improved generalization. Yet, recent studies show that policy performance can degrade substantially under changes in viewpoint, robot initialization, language, appearance, or object layout~ fei2025liberoplus . These findings raise the question of how much benchmark success reflects generalization beyond the demonstrations, and how much can be achieved through demonstration retrieval alone. Retrieval in robot learning has mainly been used for data selection, in-context adaptation, and non-parametric control. For data selection, Behavior Retrieval~ Du2023 retrieves task-relevant trajectories from large offline datasets, FlowRetrieval~ lin2025flow selects demonstrations using optical-flow-based motion similarity, and STRAP~ memmel2025strap retrieves reusable sub-trajectories from offline data to augment downstream policy training. title: DeRep: Learning Depth Representations for End-to-End Navigation in Cluttered Environments
summary: End-to-end navigation in cluttered environments relies on compact visual representations to support collision avoidance and goal-directed motion. Existing methods typically learn these representations jointly with the policy or through observation reconstruction, which does not explicitly specify what information the representation should preserve. Moreover, they are usually evaluated with a single downstream policy learner, although the benefit of a representation may depend on how the policy is learned. Modular navigation systems typically separate perception, mapping, planning, and control FastPlanner EgoPlanner . End-to-end approaches instead learn a direct mapping from depth images and robot state to actions or trajectories VitFly MAVRL . For depth-based policies, an encoder typically compresses the depth image into a latent representation on which the policy bases its decisions. Transferring a policy from simulation to the real world therefore depends in part on whether this representation continues to provide useful navigation information under conditions not encountered during training. Existing learning-based navigation methods often train the encoder jointly with the policy , allowing the downstream learning objective to shape the representation VitFly HighSpeedRL . Other methods use reconstruction-based objectives to learn depth representations, either by reconstructing the original observation MAVRL or a transformed depth image that accounts for the robot's size CollisionEnc . RELATED WORK Visual Representation Learning Visual representation learning aims to encode high-dimensional visual observations into compact features that support downstream tasks. General-purpose methods such as SimCLR~ SimCLR and DINOv2~ dinov2 learn broadly transferable features through self-supervised objectives. Robotics-oriented methods further adapt representation learning to embodied data. For example, R3M~ R3M learns reusable visual features from egocentric human videos for robot manipulation, while DeFM~ DeFM learns large-scale depth representations for transfer across robotic tasks. The usefulness of a visual representation, however, can depend strongly on the information required by the downstream task. Task-relevant representations have also been explored in embodied navigation, where tasks such as ObjectNav and PointNav involve different requirements for semantic understanding, localization, and spatial memory. title: GEMOR-GS: Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM
summary: Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation. 3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable by supplying an explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model. We present GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable, providing a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making. To improve the 3DGS map, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is first estimated offline by direct-method alignment over dedicated calibration segments and reused by all following online and offline processes. Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR--projection objective. The final global reconstruction is then rebuilt from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted. For the robot SLAM lifecycle, the method recovers the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences quantify each element: the offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3--19.9 dB, improves PSNR by approximately 9 dB over Gaussian-LIC2, and achieves 86--100% held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality. The results show that GEMOR-GS improves the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map, serving as a dependable robot world model for SLAM and downstream tasks.

In order to improve the quality of the 3DGS map, before modeling, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is estimated offline first by a direct-method LiDAR--camera alignment over dedicated calibration segments. Introduction sec:intro Background sec:intro-bg In recent years, 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) has become the dominant explicit radiance-field representation for SLAM and dense reconstruction, and LiDAR--inertial--visual (LIV) tightly coupled SLAM systems augmented with it promise robots a photorealistic and metrically consistent world representation kerbl3Dgaussians,zheng2025fastlivo2,hong2025gslivo . Beyond rendering benchmarks, 3DGS models are also increasingly deployed as world-model representations: embodied agents build Gaussian world representations of goal states for visual rearrangement melik24gaussianworld ; end-to-end driving stacks use splatting as the scene representation of a predictive world model yan2025renderworld ; and object-centric Gaussian world models learn action-conditioned rigid-body dynamics to support model predictive control kreber2026mrogwm . This trend assigns the SLAM-produced 3DGS map a more demanding role than that of an offline asset scored by rendering metrics. The map must serve as a queryable and dependable world representation that supports localization, mapping, and downstream decision-making over continuous operation. Geometric accuracy (calibration and poses), appearance fidelity (reconstruction quality), and re-enterability (relocalization) are first-order prerequisites. However, most current LIV fusion pipelines are still not queryable and dependable enough for robot SLAM and world-model deployment. Geometric accuracy demands trustworthy spatiotemporal calibration. LiDAR--camera extrinsic residuals and the nearest-pairing offset are written into every keyframe's depth--color binding, and hence into the Gaussian supervision. The ghosting observed in fused maps mixes three coupled sources: spatial extrinsic residuals, the temporal pairing offset, and pose suboptimality. The online filter produces only locally optimal Markov estimates of pose and absorbs extrinsic residuals only up to the observability limit. A trustworthy calibration should be applied to ensure the accuracy of the extrinsic. The extrinsic must be estimated before refining the poses and map. And the propagation of extrinsic quality into reconstruction and relocalization must be quantified, not just be assumed. Appearance fidelity demands a global refinement stage. The real-time budget admits only limited per-frame optimization over a field-of-view (FoV) sliding window, without densification and with low-order spherical harmonics. Therefore, the online map remains a tracking aid rather than the final reconstruction. The benefit of calibration and pose refinement must propagate into reconstruction quality, which requires a global reconstruction stage that inherits the refined calibration and poses. Re-enterability demands a recovery mechanism in the robot SLAM lifecycle. Tracking loss is inevitable in real deployments, arising from fast rotation, motion blur, lighting change, and dynamic occlusion. If the 3DGS map does not provide the ability to recover the pose, a robot cannot re-enter the map, resume mapping, or support downstream tasks. Most existing 3DGS SLAM work stops at offline rendering evaluation. For using 3DGS mapping in robot SLAM, the lifecycle of tracking, loss, recovery, and resumption would be an indispensable consideration. Objective sec:intro-contrib In this research, we present a novel method --- GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM), which is a LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM system that estimates poses under a real-time budget and archives keyframes. It upgrades the SLAM-produced 3DGS map from an offline render asset to a dependable robot world model. It is a representation whose geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability can be relied upon by localization, mapping, and downstream decision-making over continuous operation for a robot even when tracking loss occurs. In this method, for the extrinsic calibration, a direct-method module is used to estimate the LiDAR--camera extrinsic offline over dedicated calibration segments and supplies it to other modules. The offline track then refines keyframe poses and the Gaussian map alternately, purifying the depth--color supervision that drives Gaussian training. For offline mapping, a global reconstruction stage re-initializes the Gaussian model from the refined keyframe schema and executes global densification, pruning, and spherical-harmonics order elevation, turning the online sliding-window map into the final high-fidelity reconstruction. For relocalization, a bypass module matches XFeat descriptors against a lightweight relocalization database, obtains a coarse pose by RANSAC-PnP, and refines it by Gaussian RGB-D warp alignment, enabling the robot to recover its global pose after tracking loss. This work makes the following three primary contributions: A global-optimized reconstruction stage. Our method promotes the online map---a FoV sliding-window tracking aid---to the final reconstruction, so that refinements in calibration and poses translate into gains in appearance fidelity. The stage re-initializes the Gaussian model from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted, and executes global densification, pruning, and spherical-harmonics order elevation. It can make the 3DGS map more photorealistic and metrically consistent. A relocalization module for the robot SLAM lifecycle. Our method recovers the global pose from the 3DGS map through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Based on the globally optimized and reconstructed 3DGS map, the re-embedded pose can be estimated accurately enough to resume mapping and support downstream tasks. A calibration-quality-controlled mapping framework. Our method makes the geometry that supervises Gaussian training trustworthy by evaluating the quality of the extrinsic calibration offline. The extrinsic is estimated by an adopted direct-method LiDAR--camera alignment koide2023calibration over dedicated calibration segments. The residuals will be written into every keyframe's depth--color binding and pose filtering will absorb them only up to the observability limit. Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian map parameters will be refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR-projection objective. Paper Organization sec:intro-org The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:rw reviews related works, covering the background of 3D Gaussian splatting and the recent 3DGS SLAM systems. Section~ sec:method presents the method: the system overview and the three main modules: the calibration refinement module, the global reconstruction module and the relocalization module. Section~ sec:exp reports the experiments, including the setup, the extrinsic calibration evaluation, the online and offline reconstruction evaluation, and the relocalization evaluation. Section~ sec:concl concludes the paper and outlines some future directions. Related Works sec:rw 3D Gaussian Splatting sec:rw-3dgs Neural radiance fields (NeRF) mildenhall2020nerf achieved photorealistic novel view synthesis by optimizing a continuous volumetric function through differentiable ray sampling. However, the dense per-ray sampling makes training and rendering computationally expensive and thus precludes its real-time use. As an alternative, 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) kerbl3Dgaussians represents the scene explicitly as anisotropic Gaussian ellipsoids and renders them by differentiable rasterization, attaining real-time rendering at quality competitive with NeRF while keeping the representation explicit and editable. Image-only 3DGS reconstruction builds on this representation under purely photometric supervision, with camera poses and initial points typically supplied by structure-from-motion schoenberger2016sfm . Subsequent works relaxed these requirements: CF-3DGS fu2024cf3dgs progressively grows the Gaussian map frame by frame from an unposed video stream, and InstantSplat fan2024instantsplat jointly optimizes camera poses and Gaussian parameters from sparse unposed images. However, without metric depth, the geometric accuracy of these systems is bounded by photometric evidence alone. Recently, many research efforts have focused on coupling cameras with LiDAR to bring metric geometry into 3DGS reconstruction. title: RetinexGS: Retinex-Inspired Gaussian Splatting for Low-Light RAW Reconstruction
summary: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipelines struggle with severely underexposed images, producing unstable colors, floating artifacts, and incomplete reconstructions in dark regions. To better account for noise in these low-light observations, RAW images offer a natural basis for noise-aware reconstruction by preserving linear sensor measurements and providing access to noise metadata. We present RetinexGS, a RAW-domain 3DGS framework that combines Retinex-inspired appearance modeling with sensor-informed optimization for low-light novel-view synthesis. We factorize each Gaussian's color into a view-independent base color and a shared, position- and view-dependent modulation field, regularizing the two components separately to constrain appearance learning from noisy observations. We use DNG noise metadata to weight the reconstruction loss for signal-dependent noise, while distortion-aware rendering avoids spatially resampling RAW targets. To address sparse geometry in dark regions, we introduce depth-guided initialization. We evaluate RetinexGS on three public RawNeRF scenes and two custom-captured low-light RAW scenes. With all methods trained on the same RAW inputs for each scene, RetinexGS outperforms LE3D and RawNeRF in mean sRGB PSNR by 2.18 dB and 2.71 dB respectively, across the five scenes, while supporting real-time novel-view rendering.

Introduction sec:intro Novel-view synthesis (NVS) in low-light environments remains challenging for modern 3D representations. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs performs well when structure-from-motion (SfM)~ schoenberger2016sfm provides reliable initialization and well-exposed sRGB images provide stable photometric supervision. Under severely low-light conditions, feature correspondences become sparse or unreliable in dark and texture-poor regions, while sensor noise obscures weak image signals. The resulting sparse point-cloud initialization and noisy supervision can lead to incomplete geometry, unstable colors, and floating artifacts in the reconstructed scene. A natural alternative is to train 3DGS directly on RAW images, which retain high-bit-depth, approximately linear sensor measurements before image signal processing (ISP) and thus preserve information that may be lost in sRGB images. When RAW images are stored in the Digital Negative (DNG) format~ adobe2012dng , an open container for RAW sensor data, their metadata may additionally provide per-channel noise parameters (the NoiseProfile tag) that can inform noise-aware optimization. RawNeRF~ mildenhall2022rawnerf demonstrated that multi-view optimization can reconstruct scenes directly from noisy RAW observations captured in near darkness, and LE3D~ jin2024le3d extended RAW-domain reconstruction to real-time Gaussian rendering. Building on these advances, we introduce a structured appearance representation to constrain Gaussian color estimation under noisy RAW supervision. Retinex theory~ land1971lightness models appearance as the product of reflectance and illumination. Inspired by this principle, we structure Gaussian appearance multiplicatively in linear RAW space: each Gaussian carries a view-independent base color, which is multiplied by a modulation that a compact, scene-shared field predicts from the Gaussian's position and the viewing direction. Because the field is shared across the scene, it captures smooth spatial and view-dependent variation, while per-Gaussian color detail is carried by the base factor. The factorization alone is ambiguous, since scale can be traded freely between the two factors; its value lies in allowing each factor to be constrained separately. Rather than fitting a single per-Gaussian color directly to noisy observations, we can therefore impose priors suited to each factor. We propose RetinexGS, a RAW-domain framework that implements this idea through factor-specific regularization and sensor-informed optimization. We constrain the modulation scale and encourage local consistency of the base colors (Sec.~ sec:retinex ), while fitting packed RAW observations with channel-wise noise weights derived from the DNG NoiseProfile. We handle lens distortion within the rasterizer, enabling supervision directly on the packed RAW grid without spatially resampling the targets. To improve geometric coverage, we augment SfM initialization with monocular-depth samples in dark regions with insufficient SfM points. Experiments on public and newly captured low-light RAW scenes demonstrate improved reconstruction quality under both native-pipeline and matched-input comparisons, while retaining real-time rendering. Fig.~ fig:teaser provides a visual overview. Our contributions are: Our contributions are: Factored appearance for noisy RAW supervision. To constrain Gaussian color estimation under noise, we represent each Gaussian's color as the product of a view-independent base color and a modulation predicted by a scene-shared field from the Gaussian's position and the viewing direction. This factorization lets us regularize the base color and the modulation separately. The product is formed per Gaussian before alpha compositing. Sensor-informed RAW optimization. We exploit the camera's own sensor and lens properties during training. Each RAW channel is weighted by a noise level derived from the DNG NoiseProfile. Lens distortion is modeled inside the rasterizer, so the loss is computed on the original packed RAW pixels without resampling them. In addition, we use monocular depth to add initialization points in dark regions where SfM points are sparse. Evaluation on low-light RAW scenes. We demonstrate improved reconstruction quality on public and newly captured low-light RAW scenes, supported by ablations of the appearance model and of where the product is formed. Forming the product per Gaussian achieves quality comparable to multiplying rendered images, while roughly halving training time in our implementation. Related Work sec:related 3D Gaussian Splatting and appearance. 3DGS~ kerbl20233dgs represents scenes as anisotropic Gaussian primitives rendered through differentiable alpha compositing, enabling high-quality novel-view synthesis at real-time rates. Subsequent work improves geometry~ huang20242dgs,yu2024gof , anti-aliasing~ yu2024mipsplatting , and training efficiency~ mallick2024taming3dgs . Standard 3DGS represents view-dependent color using spherical harmonics coefficients. Extensions incorporate shading functions, material properties, and illumination models for inverse rendering and relighting~ gao2024relightable3dgs,jiang2024gaussianshader,liang2024gsir , while LE3D~ jin2024le3d uses a compact color network with per-Gaussian features and biases for RAW-domain rendering. Our work studies a Retinex-inspired RAW appearance representation with per-Gaussian base color, shared position- and view-conditioned modulation, and factor-specific regularization. HDR and RAW-domain reconstruction. HDR-NeRF~ huang2022hdr reconstructs HDR radiance fields from LDR images captured at different exposures, while RawNeRF~ mildenhall2022rawnerf demonstrates reconstruction directly from noisy RAW observations. LE3D~ jin2024le3d extends RAW-domain reconstruction to real-time Gaussian rendering. From Chaos to Clarity~ li2024chaos combines Gaussian reconstruction with a learned noise extractor constrained by a sensor-noise prior, whereas HDRSplat~ singh2024hdrsplat uses PMRID denoising before Gaussian optimization. RetinexGS directly fits packed noisy RAW observations using channel-wise weights derived from DNG noise metadata. Camera projection is another relevant consideration: Fisheye-GS~ liao2024fisheye extends Gaussian projection to fisheye cameras, and From Chaos to Clarity~ li2024chaos maps rendered predictions into distorted image coordinates. Our implementation incorporates lens distortion into projected Gaussian centers and covariance footprints, enabling supervision on the packed RAW grid without spatially resampling the targets. Retinex and low-light reconstruction. Single-image low-light enhancement methods use Retinex-based decomposition or learned enhancement models~ guo2017lime,wei2018retinexnet,zhang2019kind,cai2023retinexformer,guo2020zerodce,wu2022uretinex,zheng2022sgz . Applying such methods independently to individual views does not explicitly enforce multi-view consistency. Low-light neural rendering methods incorporate decomposition, illumination modeling, and physical priors into scene reconstruction~ wang2023llnerf,cui2024alethnerf,zhou2025lita . LL-Gaussian~ sun2025ll models reflectance and illumination attributes on Gaussian primitives for low-light sRGB reconstruction and enhancement, while DTGS~ ma2025beyond incorporates thermal supervision. RetinexGS focuses on factorized Gaussian appearance learned directly from noisy linear-RAW observations, combining separate appearance priors with sensor-informed supervision. Geometric priors and initialization. Standard 3DGS uses an SfM point cloud for initialization~ schoenberger2016sfm , whose coverage can be limited in low-light and texture-poor regions. Sparse-view Gaussian methods use monocular depth priors to guide geometric optimization~ xiong2024sparsegs,zhu2024fsgs,li2024dngaussian . Learned reconstruction methods such as DUSt3R, MASt3R, and Fast3R provide dense geometric estimates~ wang2024dust3r,leroy2024mast3r,yang2025fast3r , and LL-Gaussian~ sun2025ll uses learned geometric priors for low-light initialization. title: APS-VLA: Action-Guided and Future-Aware Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong generalization in robotic manipulation, yet processing dense visual tokens often incurs high inference latency. Visual token pruning offers a practical way to reduce this cost, but identifying a compact set of tokens that preserves reliable action generation remains challenging. Existing methods largely rely on static or immediate heuristic cues to estimate token importance. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from robot demonstrations while keeping the pretrained VLA backbone frozen. A lightweight Decision Influence Estimator scores tokens conditioned on current visual observations, language instructions, and robot proprioception. Its training combines two complementary signals: action supervision matches both the full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, while an auxiliary visual transition objective uses demonstrated actions to predict subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, the estimator performs a single hard selection and packing step before the policy's native action-generation procedure; the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and with $π_{0.5}$ and XR-1 on RoboCasa365 demonstrate inference acceleration with modest changes in task success. Across five real-world tasks on two dual-arm platforms, APS-VLA reduces mean policy inference latency from 137.25 to 93.25 ms, achieving a $1.47\times$ speedup with an average success rate of 61%, compared with 60% for the unpruned baseline. Together, these results support APS-VLA as a modular, plug-in framework for efficient robotic control across VLA architectures, preserving the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies use camera observations, language instructions, and robot state to generate actions across a wide range of manipulation tasks. Models such as OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and achieve this through different action-generation architectures, yet all must repeatedly process visual observations as the robot moves~ kim2024openvla,kim2025oft,intelligence2025pi05 . With multiple cameras, a policy may process hundreds of visual tokens at each decision step, even when the next action depends on a small part of the scene. Reducing this sequence can lower inference latency. The fundamental challenge lies not merely in identifying redundant tokens, but in how to capture the dynamically evolving visual cues essential for control as a task progresses, while keeping deployment efficient and non-invasive to the pretrained policy. Figure~ fig:motivation illustrates how control-relevant visual cues change within a single task. Lifting a can requires tracking its relation to the gripper, whereas placing it requires locating the basket opening. Demonstrations capture both the commanded actions and the resulting visual changes, providing complementary supervision for token selection. Existing pruning methods largely rely on static spatial redundancy, immediate instruction relevance, or heuristic importance measures~ chen2024fastv,yang2025visionzip . Although some methods incorporate temporal consistency or adapt pruning to the motion and stage of execution~ xu2025vlacache,liu2025vlapruner,pei2026vlaadp,wang2025specprune , these criteria do not necessarily preserve the task-relevant visual information needed as manipulation unfolds. Approaches that fine-tune the entire VLA backbone additionally incur substantial training and memory costs. These limitations motivate learning a lightweight selector from robot demonstrations that identifies control-relevant visual cues across task stages under a fixed token budget, while keeping the pretrained policy frozen. We introduce APS-VLA, a framework that learns visual token selection from paired actions and observations while keeping the VLA backbone frozen. Two training objectives act on the same selected representation. The first requires the frozen policy to reproduce its predictions under full visual input and to match the demonstrated actions. The second uses the selected current representation and the demonstrated action sequence to predict a feature summary of a later observation. At the center of APS-VLA is the Decision Influence Estimator (DIE), our lightweight visual token scorer (Fig.~ fig:die ). DIE combines the features of each image patch with visual context, the instruction, and normalized robot proprioception. Both objectives train this scorer through differentiable selection. At deployment, DIE scores the current tokens once, retains the highest-scoring tokens within each camera view, and packs them for the frozen policy. The future observation and demonstrated actions are used only during training. The deployed policy uses its original action head and requires no online prediction of future observations. Our contributions are threefold. Learning visual selection from demonstration trajectories. We formulate two complementary objectives for a shared visual selector. Action supervision preserves the information needed to reproduce policy and expert actions, while action-conditioned prediction supervises the same representation with the visual change observed later in the demonstration. The Decision Influence Estimator. We introduce DIE, a lightweight module that scores individual visual tokens in the context of the instruction and robot state (Figs.~ fig:method and~ fig:die ). Trained with both objectives, DIE converts a fixed budget per camera into a single hard selection step that integrates with the frozen policy's native action generator. Extensive simulation and real-world evaluation. APS-VLA achieves inference speedups of on LIBERO, on RoboCasa365, and across five real-world tasks, with task success rates close to the corresponding unpruned baselines. Upon acceptance, we will release the code for reproducing our experiments and all model checkpoints. Related Work sec:related_work token compression. Visual token compression reduces inference cost by shortening the sequence processed by a model. DynamicViT learns to discard tokens progressively, EViT fuses less-attended tokens, and ToMe merges tokens with similar features~ rao2021dynamicvit,liang2022evit,bolya2023tome . In vision-language models, FastV uses early-layer attention to identify tokens for removal, PruMerge combines selection and merging, and SparseVLM uses text to guide visual sparsification~ chen2024fastv,shang2025prumerge,zhang2025sparsevlm . CSP reduces the cost of multimodal inference by pruning the key-value cache~ pei2024csp . For robot control, visual similarity and instruction relevance capture only part of the selection problem. Patches on the same object may be equally relevant to the instruction while providing different information about grasp contact or clearance. pruning and reuse in VLA policies. Robot policies span discrete action tokens (RT-2 and FAST)~ brohan2023rt2,pertsch2025fast , action chunks (ACT)~ zhao2023act , and continuous actions generated by diffusion or flow matching~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,li2024cogact,black2024pi0 . Visual token pruning targets the observation sequence shared by these policies. VLA-Cache reuses computation for visual tokens that remain stable across frames~ xu2025vlacache . VLA-Pruner combines vision-language prefill attention with an estimate of action-decoding attention from recent steps~ liu2025vlapruner . VLA-ADP uses end-effector motion to determine when to apply text-guided pruning, while SpecPrune-VLA combines information from preceding steps with current attention and adjusts pruning according to the motion being executed~ pei2026vlaadp,wang2025specprune . SAFE-Pruner addresses a different source of error: a token assigned low importance in an early layer may be needed deeper in the network. It therefore incorporates attention cues from later layers into pruning decisions~ ma2026safepruner . These methods use signals available during policy execution. Demonstrations offer an additional signal during training because they record the physical outcome of the action taken from each observation. visual selection from robot trajectories. LightVLA makes token pruning differentiable so that the policy objective can shape the selection rule~ jiang2025lightvla , while GridS learns spatial coordinates for feature sampling via differentiable interpolation~ feng2026grids . Beyond immediate control signals, prior policy learning studies have shown the value of future visual states: UniPi and SuSIE guide control via predicted videos or image subgoals~ du2023unipi, black2024susie , GR-1 jointly predicts actions and future images~ wu2023gr1 , and Seer conditions inverse dynamics on predicted visual states~ tian2024seer . Very recently, the concurrent work VLA-ACL~ du2026vlaacl explores learning a token selector over a frozen VLA backbone using action-consistency supervision from expert demonstrations. This is closely aligned with our insight that visual token importance should be learned through its contribution to action generation. Action supervision directly tests whether the retained representation supports the immediate command. In long-horizon or unseen compositional tasks, however, distinct interaction states often call for similar motions, where the current action target alone gives limited guidance on which visual details govern how the scene will evolve. APS-VLA therefore couples action supervision with action-conditioned visual transition prediction: given the demonstrated actions, the features retained by DIE must support both the current policy output and a later visual representation. title: From Egocentric Human Video to Robot Manipulation in the Era of Embodied Intelligence
summary: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.
full_text: Introduction sec_intro Embodied intelligence studies how agents perceive, learn, and act in the physical world, with robot manipulation focusing on interactions that change object states to achieve task goals. Robot manipulation policies demand robot-object interaction experience that covers different tasks, objects, and environments~ sunderhauf_limits_2018 . Collecting this experience directly on robots requires physical platforms, repeated task execution, teleoperation, and scene setup. However, these collection requirements restrict both the scalability and variety of robot demonstrations available for policy learning~ mandlekar_mimicgen_2023, kareer_egomimic_2024 . This limitation motivates supplementing robot demonstrations with hand-object interaction (HOI) videos. Egocentric human video (EHV), recorded by human-worn cameras during everyday activities, provides such HOI experience and a potential of scalability and variety. Large-scale EHV datasets record human activities across tasks and environments without requiring a robot to perform each interaction~ damen_rescaling_2020, grauman_ego4d_2022 . In an egocentric view, the camera often records the demonstrator's hands, manipulated objects, and their changing spatial relationships at close range~ su_interformer_2026 . Its temporal structure reveals how interactions unfold, including action ordering, object state changes, and task progression. These spatial and temporal cues offer interaction priors and task information for learning visual representations and manipulation policies. Human video leaves the robot's control problem underspecified. Specifically, human hands and robot end-effectors differ in morphology and motion capabilities. Human-worn and robot-mounted cameras also observe interactions from different viewpoints. Moreover, EHV does not record robot action commands, and visual observations alone cannot fully determine the forces and contact dynamics required for execution. Existing approaches attempted to exploit EHV through cross-domain alignment of human and robot demonstrations~ kareer_egomimic_2024 and visual representation pretraining~ nair_r3m_2022 . Recently, latent action pretraining derives action-like targets from visual transitions without recorded action labels~ ye_latent_2025 . We use the term Ego2Robot learning for learning manipulation-relevant knowledge from EHV and grounding it in the capabilities of the target robot. =-1 Existing reviews address robot learning from robot demonstrations, general human videos, and embodied manipulation~ correia_survey_2023, eze_learning_2025, ma_robot_2026, ye_data_2026, zheng_survey_2025 , where the comparisons with ours are shown in Table~ tab:survey_comparison . Recently, Ma et al.~ ma_robot_2026 organize human-video-based learning into task-, observation-, and action-oriented transfer pathways. Feng et al.~ feng_human_2026 distinguish latent actions, predictive world models, and explicit 2D/3D supervision for VLA learning. Our review examines how EHV observation conditions affect robot manipulation through Ego2Robot learning. We therefore compare what information is derived, how robots use it during training or deployment, and what additional data or grounding is required. Figure~ fig:taxonomy illustrates the four learning paradigms and the data resources that support them. We distinguish four paradigms according to how human video contributes to Ego2Robot learning: 1)~explicit embodiment transfer explicitly converts EHV's human manipulation behavior into robot-format training data; 2)~explicit action and task supervision extracts interpretable signals from EHV that guide policy learning or execution; 3)~egocentric video representation pretraining learns visual representations from EHV for downstream manipulation; and 4)~latent action and dynamics modeling learns action abstractions and predictive models from EHV's visual experience. Alongside them, we consider EHV as the primary source of human experience, robot demonstrations as a source of embodiment-specific grounding, and synthetic and simulated data as resources for augmentation and physically grounded learning. The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we organize Ego2Robot learning into four paradigms and review their supporting data sources, as shown in Figure~ fig:taxonomy . Second, we compare the information used by these paradigms and examine how first-person observation constraints affect their additional supervision and grounding requirements. Third, we identify open challenges in physically feasible transfer, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control. We consider both training-time knowledge transfer and deployment-time use of demonstrations and feedback. Scope and literature selection. The core literature reviewed in this paper satisfies two criteria: it uses EHV as a source of training data, supervision, or task information, and it connects that information to robot manipulation through policy learning, planning, or execution. Studies using mixed data sources are included when their use of EHV is explicitly documented; their inclusion does not imply that reported gains can be attributed to EHV alone. We consider both peer-reviewed publications and publicly available preprints as literature in this paper. Foundational video-learning methods, perception models, robot demonstrations, and synthetic data resources are discussed as methodological context or complementary grounding rather than evidence of Ego2Robot learning in their own right. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec_main_1 presents the problem formulation and four learning paradigms. Section~ sec_main_2 reviews the supporting training data landscape. Section~ sec_challenges discusses open challenges and future directions, and Section~ sec_conclusion concludes the paper.

title: Ego Guidance: Enhancing Robot Policy Learning with Action-Free Human Egocentric Videos
summary: In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision. Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction. We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.

Introduction Embodied AI models are still in their infancy, eagerly absorbing every valuable source of world knowledge. Among these sources, human egocentric videos are particularly promising. Their large-scale availability, ease of acquisition, and close connection to the open-world environment make them an important potential source of data for embodied intelligence~ graumanEgo4DWorld30002022a,lyuLDA1BScalingLatent2026,liOpenAoEOpenEgocentric2026, sunEgo4WAMWhatMatters2026 . However, precise action annotation is expensive to acquire, making most of the resources available only in video form (which we call action-free). In this work, we investigate whether such action-free data can provide benefits to robot policy learning without action restoration. Guided by first-principled considerations, rather than adopting a World Action Model (WAM) architecture~ liangVideoGeneratorsAre2025,liLingbotVA2026,yeWorldActionModels2026a that performs diffusion in a generative latent space, we start from a simpler and well-optimized Vision Language Model (VLM) backbone, expand it into a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT), and jointly optimize the model with action and visual state prediction. Building on this Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), we investigate how different encoders for representing the predicted state affect performance. We further conduct preliminary studies on several important factors, including data cleaning, diversity trade-off, and the scalability potential of pretraining with action-free egocentric videos. Method sec:method We adopt an MoT architecture~ pi0,liang2024mot that leverages a pretrained VLM~ qwen35 to jointly model robot actions and future world states. Experiment We describe the datasets and training settings in this section. See Appendix~ app:impl for more details. Datasets Robot Data. We curate the dataset from DROID~ khazatskyDROIDLargeScaleInTheWild2024 by retaining successful episodes and filtering out episodes with no motion or without valid instruction or action annotations. This yields approximately 38,000 episodes totaling 230 hours of robot data (66 retention), which we co-train with egocentric video data. For the final real robot scenario, we extend the robot data with more datasets~ liu2023libero,chen2025robotwin2,contributors2024agibotworldrepo,internroboticsrepo,abc2026,simpleai2026hifiumi , totaling about hours, and internal demonstrations collected via tele-operation for downstream fine-tuning. Egocentric Data. We use Ego4D~ graumanEgo4DWorld30002022a for our preliminary experiments. As it does not provide usable action labels, we treat it as action-free egocentric video data. Its raw videos comprise 3,976 hours, and we describe our curation in Section~ sec:ego_data . To increase scale, we also use Open-AoE~ liOpenAoEOpenEgocentric2026 , which provides approximately 1M annotated video clip--caption pairs on 8,000 tasks, spanning 2,000 hours. For Open-AoE, we use the released clips and language descriptions following the dataset's original curation, without applying the Ego4D-specific gates. Training We compared two training strategies in the primary experiments. In single-stage training, we jointly train on the robot demonstrations that are aligned with the downstream evaluation tasks and egocentric videos. In two-stage training, we first co-train on a broader collection of robot demonstrations and egocentric videos, then fine-tune on downstream-aligned demonstrations alone. The single-stage strategy consistently yields poorer generalization, with little variation across experimental settings. This behavior suggests overfitting to the limited robot data and provides little insight into the effect of egocentric pretraining. We therefore use the two-stage strategy for SPAR as default. title: CIALLO: Learning Shared Intent Representations for Cross-Embodiment Manipulation
summary: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7\% average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0\% for fully finetuned $π_0$. In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3\% success on LIBERO and 52.7\% on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8\% on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning.
full_text: Robot demonstrations contain reusable manipulation knowledge, but transferring this knowledge across embodiments requires representations that bridge differences in control interfaces. Action reconstruction alone does not ensure that similar behaviors across robots share a representation. To address this gap, we introduce CIALLO, an action codec that aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in a shared space of short-horizon behavioral intent. An embodiment-conditioned decoder maps this intent back to robot-specific actions, allowing a shared representation to support different control interfaces. After pretraining on eight embodiments, CIALLO adapts to a new robot from one recording of at most 10 seconds by updating only its embodiment embeddings. The calibrated codec then remains frozen while a policy learns to predict intent from observations and instructions. We instantiate this policy with Qwen3.5-4B to form Qwen-CIALLO, whose backbone requires no large-scale robot-action pretraining before policy finetuning. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7 average success across real SO-101 and single-arm Piper robots, compared with 70.0 for fully finetuned . In simulation, we additionally finetune the action decoder, achieving 97.3 success on LIBERO and 52.7 on RoboTwin 2.0. The LIBERO policy also achieves 80.8 on LIBERO-Plus without further finetuning. Together, these results support a shared action codec as a transferable control interface that separates embodiment calibration from task learning. Introduction A grasp demonstrated by one robot can teach another what to reach for and how an object should move, even when their joint coordinates and control rates differ. Cross-embodiment learning seeks to reuse experience from existing robots to provide control knowledge for a new body~ oxe2023rtx,ghosh2024octo,liu2025rdt . Pretrained vision-language models supply broad semantic knowledge~ kim2024openvla,Black2024Pi0 , but grounding that knowledge in an unfamiliar action interface still requires substantial amounts of robot demonstration data. A reusable action codec could make these demonstrations more useful for task learning by reducing the need to adapt the underlying control representation. Recorded actions entangle behavior with the coordinates and control conventions used to execute it. Similar motions can be expressed as end effector displacements or joint angles, with different dimensions, numbers of arms, and temporal resolutions. Shared action layouts and embodiment-specific modules allow policies to consume heterogeneous data~ ghosh2024octo,liu2025rdt,wang2024hpt . Yet action reconstruction alone, even with embodiment-conditioned encoding and decoding, does not require similar behaviors across robots to have similar representations. Visual changes and grounded language connect different control sequences that produce similar visual effects or serve compatible task goals. We therefore align action representations through these shared cues to learn a codec that transfers across embodiments with only brief calibration. We introduce CIALLO (Cross-embodiment Intent All In One Space), an action codec for transferring control knowledge across robots. CIALLO separates a shared representation of short-horizon behavior, intent, from the body and control schema used to realize it. Building on latent action learning and action--vision alignment~ ye2025lapa,bu2025univla,zhang2026clap,chen2026unit , CIALLO aligns actions, visual changes, and observation-grounded language in one space. The visual and text branches anchor actions to their effects and task context, encouraging nearby representations for compatible behaviors across embodiments. A shared decoder reconstructs actions from all three representations, preserving the control information needed to execute them (Figure~ fig:teaser A). An essential vector , arm and axis embeddings, and execution times supply the embodiment-specific context. The same codec weights therefore support different action dimensions, control rates, and single- or dual-arm configurations. The aligned action codec then provides the interface for policy learning. From one recording of at most 10 seconds, we fit only the new robot's essential vector and arm and axis embeddings, keeping the shared network fixed. We freeze the calibrated codec and train a policy to predict intent from observations and instructions. The action encoder and decoder supervise this prediction (Figure~ fig:teaser B--C). Calibration establishes how the codec realizes behavior on the new body, while task demonstrations teach the policy which intent to produce. We pair the codec with Qwen3.5-4B~ qwen35blog through StarVLA~ starvla2026 , forming Qwen-CIALLO without large-scale robot-action pretraining of the Qwen backbone. We pretrain CIALLO on eight embodiments and evaluate reuse on real SO-101 and single-arm Piper configurations absent from pretraining (Piper pretraining uses a simulated dual-arm configuration). Calibration takes approximately 30 minutes per robot, after which the codec remains frozen. With 20 demonstrations per task, Qwen-CIALLO achieves 76.7 average success, compared with 70.0 for fully finetuned . In simulation, where the action decoder is also finetuned, Qwen-CIALLO reaches 97.3 on LIBERO after 10k policy steps and 80.8 on LIBERO-Plus without further training. One policy trained jointly on RoboTwin 2.0 achieves 52.7 after 40k steps. These evaluations test both adaptation to new robots and policy learning across tasks with the shared action codec. title: FAME-QP: A GPU-Accelerated Quadratic-Programming Solver for Real-Time Model Predictive Control
summary: We present FAME-QP, a GPU-accelerated solver for dense quadratic programs arising in linear model predictive control. FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. It probes a cached operator bank to select the initial penalty and updates operators lazily when problem matrices change. Numerical benchmarks and simulated humanoid and quadrotor control experiments demonstrate reduced latency relative to competing GPU solvers while maintaining solution accuracy and control performance.

FAME-QP combines constraint-dependent operator representations with fused single- and two-kernel iterations replayed through CUDA graphs, automatically selecting the execution configuration through device calibration and problem-specific timing. Introduction Quadratic programming (QP) problems arise in a wide range of applications, including statistics, machine learning, finance, and model predictive control (MPC) for robotic and control systems turlach2015quadratic, stellato2020osqp, wensing2023optimization . They also appear as subproblems in nonlinear optimization algorithms, such as sequential quadratic programming (SQP). Many of these applications lead to convex QP problems. Among these applications, MPC requires solving an optimization problem within each control sampling period, making computational efficiency critical for real-time operation wang2010fast . With linear prediction models, convex quadratic costs, and linear constraints, each MPC update requires solving a convex QP problem, yielding a formulation commonly referred to as linear MPC (LMPC). Common solution approaches for QP problems include interior-point (IP), active-set (AS), operator-splitting (OS), and proximal methods. Representative IP methods include HPIPM frison2020hpipm , qpSWIFT pandala2019qpswift , PIQP schwan2023piqp , and Clarabel goulart2026clarabel (with QP as a special case). Although IP methods often converge in relatively few iterations, each iteration requires solving a potentially expensive linear system. They are also generally more difficult to warm start, limiting their ability to exploit similarities between successive QP problems in MPC bishop2024reluqp . AS methods, such as qpOASES ferreau2014qpoases and DAQP arnstrom2022daqp , readily support warm starting and can be highly efficient when initialized with the correct active set. However, their combinatorial worst-case complexity in the number of constraints can limit their scalability to large-scale QPs bishop2024reluqp . OS methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), such as OSQP stellato2020osqp , and related proximal methods, such as ProxQP bambade2022proxqp , are increasingly used in robotic MPC owing to their ease of warm starting and suitability for applications requiring moderate solution accuracy schubiger2020cuosqp,dinh2025real . Moreover, their computational structure offers opportunities for parallelization. Nevertheless, their convergence rates can be slower than those of other methods, particularly when high-accuracy solutions are required schwan2023piqp . Although most established QP solvers are CPU-based, GPUs offer opportunities to accelerate large-scale QP solving through massive parallelism and higher memory bandwidth, enabling concurrent execution of independent computations and faster data movement schubiger2020cuosqp . Growing interest in MPC for robotics and control using world models hansen2024td, rajkumar2026kpwm , locally linear latent dynamics watter2015embed , and Koopman-based linear, bilinear, or semi-linear representations korda2018linear,goswami2021bilinearization,rajkumar2025real further motivates GPU acceleration to meet the real-time computational demands of large-scale MPCs. Moreover, modern robotics increasingly relies on GPUs for parallel simulation, inference, and learning makoviychuk2021isaac,rudin2022learning,oneill2024open . Integrating CPU-native QP solvers into such pipelines can introduce additional latency through frequent CPU–GPU data transfers lu2025mpax . Together, these considerations motivate GPU-native QP solvers that keep optimization data and computations on the device. This work presents , Fused ADMM with Multimode Execution for QP solution, a GPU solver for the dense QPs of linear MPC. Its contributions are: (i) constraint-dependent operator representations that reduce operator storage by up to and iteration time by up to , relative to treating all constraint rows as dense; (ii) fused single- and two-kernel iterations with CUDA graph replay and automatic selection using device calibration and problem-specific timing; (iii) initial penalty selection through cached-operator probing and lazy operator updates for changing QP matrices; (iv) numerical and simulated robotic MPC evaluations demonstrating lower latency than the competing GPU methods evaluated in each benchmark, with matched solution accuracy on random QPs and comparable closed-loop control performance; and (v) an open-source implementation. title: Cognitive Multi-Agent Search and Rescue: Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collaborative Robotics
summary: Effective search and rescue (SAR) operations require autonomous systems capable of coordinating multiple heterogeneous agents, adapting to dynamic hazards, and aligning with human mission intent. Existing language-guided reinforcement learning (RL) methods primarily focus on single-agent instruction following and lack mechanisms for team-level coordination in complex, partially observable environments. This paper presents a Cognitive Multi-Agent Framework based on Language-Grounded Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (LG-HRL) that integrates natural-language understanding, hierarchical policy decomposition, and a shared cognitive workspace to achieve cohesive multi-agent behavior in SAR scenarios. Human instructions are interpreted by a large language model (LLM) and transformed into structured semantic cues that guide high-level strategy selection and role assignment across UAV and UGV agents. A formal Language-Grounded Multi-Agent Hierarchical Decision Process (LG-MAHDP) is introduced to model the interplay between semantic grounding, hierarchical control, and distributed coordination. Comprehensive experiments in a simulated disaster environment show that LG-HRL improves learning speed by 2.3 times, increases coordination coherence by 37%, and enhances subgoal accuracy and hazard avoidance by 46% and 31%, respectively. The system achieves 20-30% higher victim rescue rates, demonstrates emergent role specialization, and adapts immediately to human verbal updates. Ablation studies confirm that both the shared cognitive workspace and language grounding are critical to overall system performance. Overall, this work establishes a new paradigm for language-guided multi-agent SAR robotics, demonstrating that semantic grounding combined with hierarchical reasoning enables safer, more efficient, and more interpretable autonomous rescue operations.

title: WAM is capable in BEHAVIOR-1K: the 2nd-place solution to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge

summary: This work presents the 2nd-place solution (Team IF1001) to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge, which evaluates mobile manipulation across 100 household tasks. Our method is built on a powerful world action model (WAM), Cosmos 3. We improve Cosmos 3 by using richer visual history, task-progress conditioning, and task-group and skill-specific LoRA adapters. During inference, we apply a separate progress estimator to supply task-progress context, and use task- and progress-conditioned routing to select a task-group or skill-specific policy, complemented by action-candidate aggregation, rolling inpainting, and task-specific temporal and gripper control. To meet the minimum inference requirement of 1 FPS, we use neither recursive self-improvement (RSI) nor agentic harness methods and rely on no closed-source models; during official private-test evaluation, our system handled concurrent requests across 100 evaluation ports with limited hardware resources, sustaining an average end-to-end inference rate above 2 FPS per port. Our method achieves a mean Q-score of 0.613 and a full-task success rate of 40.9%, averaged over 3 self-evaluation rounds across all 100 tasks. On the official private test set, with 20 instances per task, our system achieves a mean Q-score of 0.615 and a full-task success rate of 41.2%.
