Introduction Building a robot with long-horizon household capabilities is a core goal in embodied AI. A household task generally requires navigation between rooms, coordinated manipulation of several objects, and a sequence of operations whose success depends on earlier actions. Small control errors can accumulate, and similar observations may call for different actions at different stages. The BEHAVIOR Challenge provides a setting for studying these difficulties through long-horizon activities in realistic household environments li2024,behavior2026 . The leading solutions to the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge build on the vision-language-action (VLA) model and demonstrate the importance of policy adaptation through training data, task-progress estimation, and execution strategies bai2025,larchenko2025 . However, due to limited training data and generalization capability, VLA models often suffer from poor instruction-following and spatial-understanding abilities. In this work, we present a WAM-based method, the 2nd-place solution, to the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge. In this solution, we adopt Cosmos 3~ nvidia2026 as our WAM backbone. We choose Cosmos 3 as our foundation model because it jointly models understanding and generation and has undergone large-scale pretraining. Cosmos 3 possesses strong language and visual reasoning capabilities while being capable of generating high-fidelity videos and actions. enhance Cosmos 3 by integrating richer visual history, task-progress estimation, and task-group LoRA fine-tuning to address observational ambiguity at complementary levels. History and progress estimation help distinguish visually similar observations possibly encountered at different task stages, while task grouping separates tasks with similar initial scene configurations but different required continuations. To improve manipulation reliability, we train separate LoRA adapters for picking, placing, opening, and closing on skill-specific demonstration segments pooled across tasks. Skill predictions from the progress estimator guide the router in selecting these skill-specific LoRA adapters. improve the inference pipeline by combining task-progress estimation, action-candidate aggregation, and rolling inpainting with task-specific execution windows, temporal retiming, and gripper-aware control. evaluate the main design choices and system configurations. Specifically, we evaluate the base policy, task-group LoRA fine-tuning, and several execution configurations, and report both partial goal completion and full-task success. The comparisons characterize the performance of the assembled system; they do not isolate the contribution of every component. In conclusion, this work demonstrates that WAM is a capable solution and has considerable potential for long-horizon household tasks such as those in the BEHAVIOR Challenge. title: LaST0.5: A Generalist World Action Model with Interaction-Centric Latent Reasoning
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation, endowing policies with strong capabilities for modeling temporal and physical dynamics. Existing WAMs, encompassing both video-first action prediction and joint video-action modeling, directly transfer global physical representations from world models to action generation. However, global scene representations may underemphasize local robot-object interactions, creating a mismatch between representations optimized for world evolution and those required for manipulation. To bridge this gap, we propose LaST0.5, a novel WAM that introduces an interaction-centric physical representation between world modeling and action generation. Specifically, LaST0.5 learns a compact interaction-centric latent space under the supervision of visual interaction cues between the robot and the environment. This reasoning space is instantiated as a latent expert that bridges the world expert and the action expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture. Furthermore, LaST0.5 performs adaptive world-to-action transfer by jointly predicting future representations and progress values, using progress consistency to adjust action execution and trigger future resampling. Finally, we pretrain LaST0.5 on a large-scale robotic data corpus comprising over 14k hours of data, establishing interaction-centric physical reasoning as a scalable and effective paradigm. LaST0.5 achieves 99.5% on LIBERO, surpasses the previous state of the art on ten evaluated RLBench tasks, and demonstrates robust long-horizon execution and precise dexterous manipulation in real-world experiments.

Introduction Building general-purpose robotic foundation models requires policies not only to understand the current scene but also to reason about how the physical world evolves under robot actions. While Vision-Language-Action (VLA)~ kim2024openvla,kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodelsoptimizing,liu2025hybridvla,intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld,2025_6_02_Fast_in_Slow,gu2025manualvla,qu2025spatialvla models have achieved strong performance by directly mapping visual observations to actions, World Action Models (WAMs)~ yuan2026fast,ye2026world,ye2026gigaworld,bi2026motus,ye2026world further augment this paradigm with world modeling, enabling policies to leverage temporal causality, implicit physics, and motion priors learned from video data. By jointly modeling world evolution and robot actions, WAMs provide a more generalizable and transferable paradigm for robotic learning~ kim2026cosmos . Despite these advantages, effectively translating world knowledge into robot actions remains an open challenge. Existing WAMs can be broadly categorized into two paradigms: Imagine-then-Execute, which first predicts future observations and then infers actions through inverse dynamics~ li2026causal,du2023learning,hu2024video,feng2026harmowam , and Joint Modeling, which jointly predicts future observations and robot actions~ bi2026motus,ye2026world,yuan2026fast,luo2026being . As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser , both paradigms share a common assumption: representations optimized for modeling world evolution inherently facilitate action generation. Although world modeling provides rich physical knowledge for manipulation, its global prediction objective may underemphasize the fine-grained robot–object interactions required for precise manipulation. Consequently, directly transferring global world representations may not fully exploit the physical knowledge required for action generation, motivating an interaction-centric physical abstraction that bridges world modeling and robot actions. To bridge this gap, we propose LaST , a generalist WAM built upon an Interaction-Centric Latent Reasoning (ICLR) framework, as shown in Figure~ fig:teaser . Unlike existing WAMs that directly transfer global world representations to action generation, LaST first learns a compact latent space that transforms global world representations into interaction-relevant physical abstractions. This reasoning space is instantiated as a latent expert within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture~ liang2024mixture , receiving global representations from a pretrained video world expert~ ali2025world . To construct interaction-centric latent supervision, future frames are augmented with interaction visual cues encoding manipulation motion and target-object affordance, and encoded by a native vision encoder into latent targets. These latent targets encourage the latent expert to learn compact physical representations centered on robot-environment interactions. Conditioned on this latent space, the efficient action expert generates precise robot actions. Overall, LaST follows a hierarchical reasoning paradigm that progressively transforms global world representations into interaction-centric abstractions and ultimately into robot actions. Furthermore, we introduce an Adaptive World-to-Action Transfer (AWAT) mechanism that enables the world model to jointly predict future representations and their corresponding progress values. Since fluctuations in world modeling accuracy can directly compromise action generation, AWAT identifies future frames with increasing progress values and executes only the temporally aligned actions from the corresponding action chunks, using progress consistency to dynamically determine the execution horizon. In real-world deployments, we validate the effectiveness of the interaction-centric latent reasoning in LaST across four bimanual tasks using the Tianji robot. LaST demonstrates robust long-horizon execution and precise control on challenging manipulation tasks. It also exhibits zero-shot generalization to unseen objects, backgrounds, and object positions, further validating the capability and robustness of our unified world-to-interaction-to-action modeling design. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We bridge the gap between global scene modeling in world models and the interaction-centric reasoning required for action generation by introducing LaST , a generalist WAM with an Interaction-Centric Latent Reasoning (ICLR) framework. We introduce the Adaptive World-to-Action Transfer (AWAT) mechanism, which jointly predicts future representations and their corresponding progress values to dynamically assess the reliability of world knowledge, to adapt action execution and trigger future resampling based on progress consistency. We pretrain LaST on a massive corpus of over 14k hours of robotic data, achieving SOTA results on simulation benchmarks (99.5 on LIBERO and 88.0 on the ten evaluated RLBench tasks) and demonstrating exceptional long-horizon execution and precise manipulation in real-world tasks. Related Work World Action Models for Robotic Manipulation World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation by leveraging temporal dynamics and physical priors learned from large-scale video generation models. Existing approaches mainly follow imagine-then-execute pipelines that ground predicted visual evolution into executable actions~ du2023learning,bharadhwaj2024gen2act,jang2025dreamgenunlockinggeneralizationrobot,feng2026harmowam , or joint video-action modeling that predicts future observations and robot actions within a unified framework~ bi2026motus,ye2026world,kim2026cosmos,li2026causal . In contrast, LaST introduces interaction-centric latent reasoning to distill global world knowledge into compact physical abstractions tailored for manipulation. Existing approaches introduce visual cues including points, sketches, and spatial annotations to specify task-relevant interaction regions, enabling more precise robot control~ liu2024moka,yuan2024robopoint,sundaresan2024rt,gu2025manualvla . title: DexSeed: Expanding Human Hand-Object Interactions into Robot Demonstrations for Dexterous Policy Learning
summary: We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples. Meanwhile, human hand--object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions. Turning these interactions into VLA training data further requires coverage of different objects and manipulation locations, together with executable arm and finger actions, and visual observations. To achieve this, we present DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot data from human hand--object interactions. Our key idea is to expand human sequences while preserving their grasps and realizing the resulting motions under arm-tracking dynamics in physics simulation. Specifically, we organize source sequences by grasp mode with shared language descriptions. InteractionMesh-based retargeting and arm trajectory augmentation adapt these sequences to the robot hand, different object geometries, and pick-and-place locations while preserving local hand--object relationships. An RL finger-control policy produces executable rollouts, while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories. Rendered observations and recorded actions from successful rollouts are paired with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA. Experiments show improved contact fidelity in retargeting and more reliable whole-arm execution than the evaluated baselines. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment further demonstrate that a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated demonstrations can execute language-specified grasps. Introduction sec:intro Dexterous hands enable robots to manipulate objects through coordinated finger motion and rich hand--object contacts. Vision-language-action (VLA) models learn to map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, providing a framework for learning manipulation skills from demonstrations~ 24arxiv_pi0 . Applying these models to dexterous manipulation requires diverse robot data that capture coordinated arm and finger actions together with visual observations and language instructions. In this work, we study how to generate physically executable robot demonstrations at scale to support dexterous VLA learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods expand robot datasets across object poses, scene layouts, and motion trajectories, but typically rely on teleoperated demonstrations as their starting point~ 23corl_mimicgen,25icra_dexmimicgen,25rss_demogen . Collecting these source demonstrations is costly for dexterous hands, as teleoperation requires coordinating many joints while maintaining stable hand--object contact~ 20icra_dexpilot,23rss_anyteleop,24corl_opentelevision . Reusing existing human hand--object datasets offers an alternative source of diverse manipulation behaviors without collecting new teleoperated demonstrations~ 20eccv_grab,22cvpr_oakink . Retargeting and physics-based imitation methods transfer these interactions to robots by addressing differences in hand morphology and contact dynamics~ 25arxiv_spider,25cvpr_maniptrans,25iclr_dextrack,26arxiv_toporetarget,26arxiv_c2dex,26arxiv_regrind,26arxiv_doasido . Expanding these transferred interactions into VLA training datasets requires varying object geometries and manipulation locations while retaining the demonstrated grasps. Such variations can alter hand--object contacts, and arm-tracking errors during execution can further disrupt the intended interaction. The resulting demonstrations must therefore preserve the grasp across these variations and provide physically executable arm and finger actions paired with visual observations. To address this need, we propose , a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot demonstrations from human interactions. Our key idea is to organize human interactions by grasp, expand them while preserving hand--object relationships, and obtain executable demonstrations through reinforcement learning with the robot arm included in simulation. Specifically, we group human sequences by grasp similarity and select representative modes, each paired with a shared description of how to grasp. InteractionMesh-based retargeting~ 12humanoids_interactionmesh first adapts the sequence to the robot hand and compatible object geometries while preserving local hand--object relationships. We combine the resulting hand references with whole-arm pick-and-place trajectories for different object starting positions and placement targets. To realize these references under arm-tracking dynamics, we train an RL finger-control policy in IsaacLab~ isaaclab while the robot arm tracks precomputed joint trajectories, allowing the policy to learn finger corrections under the resulting wrist-tracking errors. We render observations from the policy's successful rollouts and pair them with the recorded robot actions and corresponding grasp descriptions to form training demonstrations. The resulting data are used to fine-tune a VLA that jointly controls the arm and fingers to execute language-specified grasps. We select representative grasp modes from the GRAB dataset 20eccv_grab and use source sequences from these modes to generate a robot-centric dataset of demonstrations. Compared with baselines, our retargeting method better preserves the intended hand--object interactions, while our physics-based imitation achieves more reliable execution of augmented references with variations in object geometry and trajectory. We further show that a dexterous VLA fine-tuned exclusively on our simulation-generated demonstrations with rendered observations can be deployed on a real robot without collecting real-robot action demonstrations. The contributions of this work are as follows. We present a framework that groups human interactions by grasp mode and expands individual sequences into diverse robot demonstrations paired with language descriptions of how to grasp. We develop an InteractionMesh-based data generation method that preserves hand--object interactions during retargeting and transfer across different object geometries. For each source sequence, a physics-based imitation policy is jointly trained on its augmented references to obtain executable robot rollouts. We construct a robot-centric dataset of demonstrations from human sequences spanning representative grasp modes, and demonstrate its utility through simulation evaluation and real-world deployment of a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated data, without real-robot action demonstrations at deployment. Related Work sec:related Dexterous Manipulation Data Dexterous robot learning relies on diverse demonstrations that capture high-dimensional hand actions, contact-rich object motion, and robot-centric observations. Existing data sources include human hand--object datasets~ 20eccv_grab,22cvpr_oakink,24cvpr_oakink2 , direct robot teleoperation~ 20icra_dexpilot,23rss_anyteleop,24corl_opentelevision , and systems for capturing interactions or generating synthetic demonstrations~ 24arxiv_dexcap,25arxiv_dexumi,25rss_dex1b . Human datasets contain diverse grasping and manipulation behaviors, while demonstrations collected directly on robots provide robot actions and observations but are costly to collect at scale. Our work turns human hand--object interactions into executable robot data for policy learning. Human-to-robot Transfer and Physical Realization Human-to-robot transfer methods convert human hand--object demonstrations into robot motion references while accounting for differences in hand morphology~ 22eccv_dexmv,22arxiv_dextransfer,25cvpr_maniptrans,25arxiv_hermes, 25arxiv_spider,26arxiv_deximit,26arxiv_doasido . Interaction-mesh-based methods preserve local spatial relationships between the body and surrounding objects during motion retargeting~ 12humanoids_interactionmesh,25arxiv_omniretarget . Concurrent work applies related formulations to dexterous hands to preserve hand--object geometry and contact relationships~ 26arxiv_toporetarget,26arxiv_c2dex . Physics-based imitation and residual control further turn these motion references into executable robot behaviors~ 25cvpr_maniptrans,26arxiv_regrind,26arxiv_c2dex . Building on these techniques, we adapt each human source sequence to compatible object shapes and different arm trajectories to generate robot demonstrations that retain the demonstrated grasp. title: Koopman Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
summary: We propose a Koopman model-based reinforcement learning (K-MBRL) algorithm for controlling nonlinear robotic systems with unknown dynamics. The K-MBRL learns a control policy by minimizing an approximate policy objective that combines the analytical immediate cost with an estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step predicted state. To this end, we develop a stochastic Koopman operator-based learning method to approximate the unknown nonlinear dynamics in a linear representation, while a critic function estimates the remaining future cost. This formulation offers two key advantages. First, the linear Koopman dynamics simplify the model-dependent policy gradient computation to a constant matrix product, enabling computationally efficient policy improvement. Second, one-step model propagation mitigates the accumulation of prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts while retaining long-term cost information through the critic. The learned policy enables real-time control through feedforward evaluation without online optimization. We establish policy learning convergence guarantees under standard stochastic approximation assumptions. Simulations on HalfCheetah and quadruped four-legged locomotion tasks demonstrate strong sample efficiency and improved performance compared with classical model-free and model-based reinforcement learning baselines. A pendulum swing-up task is used to assess policy gradient approximation accuracy and conduct ablation studies on the learning mechanism and key hyperparameters. The proposed K-MBRL is further validated on a physical quadruped robot performing a challenging sequence of maneuvers: rising to an upright posture supported by two rounded rear feet, maintaining balance during bipedal walking, and safely returning to the ground, as shown in Fig.1.

Introduction sec:introduction Learning-based control has become a promising approach for controlling complex robotic systems whose system dynamics are unknown or difficult to model accurately. In particular, reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of robotic tasks kober2013reinforcement , including legged locomotion hutter2016anymal and manipulation li2024reinforcement . Many of these advances rely on model-free RL (MFRL) sutton2018reinforcement , which avoids explicit dynamics modeling but typically requires substantial interaction data for policy learning m2023model . Such policies are often obtained in simulation before deployment on physical robots. In contrast, classical model-based optimal control methods, such as the linear quadratic regulator and model predictive control (MPC) anderson2007optimal , can achieve effective closed-loop control without training data when accurate system dynamics are available. However, obtaining accurate dynamics models for robotic systems remains challenging due to nonlinearities, underactuation, intermittent contact, unmodeled actuator dynamics, and variations in payload and terrain spong2006robot . Model-based RL (MBRL) enjoys both benefits of MFRL and model-based optimal control by learning the dynamics from interaction data and using the learned model for policy improvement doya2000reinforcement . Its improved sample efficiency over MFRL makes it a promising approach for robotic control applications where collecting physical interaction data is costly. Many existing MBRL methods rely on multi-step model propagation for policy gradient estimation and optimization sutton1990integrated, deisenroth2011learning, janner2019trust or online planning nagabandi2018neural, chua2018deep, hansen2022temporal, askari2025model . Along these methods, prediction errors can accumulate over the rollout horizon, leading to inaccurate cost estimates and potentially biased policy gradients tanaka1996approach . Moreover, the nonlinear deep neural networks (DNNs) commonly used for dynamics learning hernandaz1990neural, draeger1995model can make repeated model propagation and differentiation computationally expensive, particularly for online policy improvement on physical robots nan2026efficient . Observation of these two limitations motivates us to develop a new framework for MBRL based on the following two key ideas. Second, we introduce a deep Koopman model (DKM) to approximate the unknown dynamics based on the Koopman operator and deep neural networks (DNN). These considerations motivate the integration of policy learning with one-step predictions from linear Koopman dynamics for efficient policy optimization. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: A Koopman model-based reinforcement learning (K-MBRL) algorithm is developed for iterative policy optimization of nonlinear systems. The optimal policy is approached iteratively along with approximating the system dynamics and estimating the policy objective. The algorithm approximates the policy objective by combining the analytical immediate cost with a state-action critic estimate of the future cost evaluated at the one-step state predicted by the learned deep Koopman model (DKM). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method to integrate stochastic DKM learning with state-action critic-based policy optimization. The linear DKM facilitates policy gradient computation, while one-step propagation mitigates the accumulation of model prediction errors associated with long-horizon rollouts. The proposed K-MBRL algorithm is validated through simulations on complex nonlinear robotic systems and challenging indoor and outdoor bipedal locomotion experiments on a physical quadruped robot, demonstrating improved control performance, faster convergence, and lower computational cost compared with baseline methods. title: DepthGS: Depth-Guided Gaussian Splatting with Adaptive Regularization for High-Quality Surface Reconstruction
comment: To appear in IEEE Trans. on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
summary: Recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient representation for novel view synthesis, offering fast differentiable rendering and high visual fidelity, and has increasingly been extended to surface reconstruction. However, the relationship between depth information and reconstruction error remains insufficiently explored, limiting the principled design of geometric optimization strategies. To fill the above gap, we propose DepthGS, a depth-guided Gaussian splatting framework. We derive theoretical relations between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error under single-view and multi-view settings, and rigorously establish corresponding upper bounds on reconstruction error. The above analysis informs the design of adaptive regularization strategies in both single-view and multi-view optimization. More specifically, for single-view optimization, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy that modulates the normal constraint strength using a geometric reliability weight computed from local depth differences. For multi-view optimization, we introduce a cross-view depth consistency regularization strategy that promotes consistency between neighboring-view depth maps and the corresponding depth predictions obtained by transforming the current view's depth predictions into those neighboring views. Extensive experiments on DTU, Mip-NeRF360, and Tanks and Temples demonstrate that DepthGS achieves competitive performance in both surface reconstruction and novel view synthesis.

INTRODUCTION Multi-view 3D reconstruction plays a crucial role in computer vision, with applications ranging from robotics~ GARAD-SLAM,Dy3DGS-SLAM,wakulicz2021active and autonomous driving~ eiffert2022resource,wang2024slam,AutoSplat to augmented and virtual reality~ lianggus_ir,wangmba_slam,yin_ms_nerf . Neural radiance fields (NeRFs)~ mildenhall2021nerf,TD-NeRF,Super-NeRF represent scenes using continuous radiance fields and achieve high-quality novel view synthesis and geometric reconstruction. However, their computationally expensive volume rendering limits real-time applications. In contrast, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d represents scenes using explicit anisotropic Gaussians and enables efficient optimization and real-time high-fidelity rendering through differentiable -blending. Despite its advances in rendering speed and quality, 3DGS still faces challenges in accurate surface reconstruction. The inherent irregularity of Gaussian primitives makes it difficult to precisely fit real-world surfaces, which may lead to geometric artifacts~ chengtopo4D . Geometry-aware approaches~ li2024geogaussian,cheng2024gaussianpro improve Gaussian representations through additional geometric constraints, while recent methods incorporating depth and normal cues ~ turkulainen2024dn,chen2024pgsr,chen2025vcr demonstrate the effectiveness of such geometric information for surface reconstruction. Nevertheless, the reconstruction errors of the three-dimensional points obtained from unbiased depth and rendered distance through inverse projection have not been explicitly characterized with respect to the corresponding ground-truth surface points. Moreover, the cross-view consistency of these two depth representations remains underexplored. These limitations motivate us to derive reconstruction-error bounds and use the resulting depth discrepancies to guide adaptive geometric regularization. In this paper, we propose DepthGS, a depth-guided Gaussian splatting framework with adaptive regularization for high-quality surface reconstruction. Through mathematical analysis, we investigate the relationship between depth information and reconstruction error and derive the corresponding upper bounds. Based on the single-view analysis, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy. For multi-view scenes, we propose a cross-view depth consistency regularization strategy to constrain depth discrepancies between neighboring views and improve multi-view geometric consistency. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Through mathematical analysis, we derive the relationships between depth discrepancies and reconstruction error under single-view and multi-view conditions, together with the upper bounds for reconstruction error, providing theoretical guidance for the subsequent optimization strategies. Based on the single-view error analysis, we propose a depth-difference-guided adaptive normal regularization strategy that modulates the normal constraint strength according to the local depth difference. Specifically, weaker constraints are applied to regions with larger depth differences, whereas stronger constraints are applied to regions with smaller depth differences. Based on the multi-view error analysis, we propose a cross-view depth consistency regularization strategy that reduces depth discrepancies between neighboring views, thereby improving multi-view geometric consistency. Extensive experiments on Mip-NeRF360~ barron2022mip , DTU~ jensen2014large and Tanks and Temples~ knapitsch2017tanks demonstrate that DepthGS achieves competitive performance in both novel view synthesis and surface reconstruction. RELATED WORK Novel View Synthesis Novel view synthesis aims to render unseen views while preserving scene structure and visual details. Classical Structure-from-Motion and Multi-View Stereo methods recover scene geometry through multi-view correspondences and epipolar constraints~ schonberger2016structure . Soft3D~ penner2017soft introduces a differentiable density-field representation for view synthesis, while NeRF and its variants represent scenes using continuous radiance fields and achieve high-quality rendering~ deng_fov_nerf,huang_ltm_nerf . However, their volumetric formulations generally incur considerable computational costs. 3DGS provides an efficient alternative by representing scenes using explicit anisotropic Gaussians and differentiable rasterization~ efficient_geometric,GeoRGS . Subsequent approaches improve representation compactness and rendering efficiency~ Compact_3D_Gaussian,Steepest_Descent,mallick2024taming , enhance structural integrity and large-scale rendering~ shen2024topology,feng2025flashgs , and extend Gaussian representations to dynamic scenes~ Motion-Aware,Fov-GS . Nevertheless, improvements in rendering quality and efficiency do not necessarily ensure accurate and view-consistent surface geometry. Gaussian Splatting Surface Reconstruction With the increasing use of Gaussian splatting in novel view synthesis, its potential for surface reconstruction has also been explored. 2DGS~ huang20242d replaces volumetric Gaussian ellipsoids with planar Gaussian disks to achieve more consistent geometric representations, while GOF~ yu2024gaussian extracts surfaces from Gaussian opacity fields. Recent approaches further improve reconstruction through geometry-oriented representations and surface constraints. GFSGS~ jiang2025geometry and GSDF~ yu2024gsdf introduce geometry-aware fields and distance representations to regularize Gaussian optimization. GS-Pull~ zhang2024gspull and GS-UDF~ li2025gaussianudf infer signed or unsigned distance functions from Gaussian primitives. QGS~ zhang2025quadratic models surfaces using second-order geometric primitives, while GSPrior~ noda20263d incorporates self-constrained geometric priors for high-fidelity surface reconstruction. Methods incorporating depth and normal cues provide complementary geometric information. DN-Splatter~ turkulainen2024dn incorporates depth and normal priors for Gaussian splatting and meshing. VCR-GauS~ chen2025vcr couples depth and normal information through a view-consistent regularizer. PGSR~ chen2024pgsr introduces unbiased-depth rendering and multi-view regularization for efficient and high-fidelity surface reconstruction. These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of depth and normal cues for geometric regularization. However, existing Gaussian splatting methods incorporating depth and normal cues do not explicitly derive reconstruction-error bounds that involve the discrepancy between unbiased depth and rendered distance. Moreover, the multi-view consistency of these two depth representations across neighboring views remains underexplored. DepthGS addresses these limitations by deriving the relationships between depth discrepancies and reconstruction errors under single-view and multi-view conditions. title: Elastic-WAM: Adaptive Spatiotemporal Imagination for Efficient Robot Control
summary: World-Action Models improve robot control by predicting future visual dynamics, but iterative video denoising incurs substantial inference overhead. Recent approaches reduce this cost through partial future denoising, yet typically rely on fixed refinement budgets. Our empirical observations reveal that preferred refinement depths vary across tasks and states, while different future regions exhibit varying relevance to action generation. Motivated by these findings, we propose Elastic-WAM, which adaptively allocates world refinement computation across temporal denoising time and spatial future space. A unified spatiotemporal refinement demand field governs when to stop world refinement, how far to advance each denoising step, and which regions to refresh. We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes, and learn it through a three-stage action-grounded supervised procedure. At inference, the learned field guides recurrent sparse world refinement to improve task success while reducing inference overhead. Evaluations across diverse simulation benchmarks and real-world long-horizon manipulation demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance with reduced inference latency.

Project page: Introduction sec:intro World-Action Models (WAMs) have shown that predicting future visual dynamics can improve robot control~ ye2026world,bi2026motus,agarwal2026cosmos,team2026motubrain,chen2026objectworld . However, iterative denoising of future videos incurs substantial inference overhead~ akbari2026flash,li2026slip . Recent studies show that intermediate video representations can already support action prediction without complete denoising~ pai2025mimic,ma2026dit4dit,li2026causal . Explicit video generation can even be removed at inference while retaining future prediction as a training objective~ yuan2026fast . Nevertheless, these approaches typically adopt a fixed future refinement budget, regardless of the current task or execution state~ guo2026unified,chen2026mvg . Consequently, a fixed budget may waste computation in some states while limiting action quality in others~ sun2026sants . To investigate this limitation, we examine how future video refinement affects downstream action quality across different tasks and states on 10 selected tasks from LIBERO-Plus benchmark~ fei25libero-plus . As demonstrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser (a.1), the number of denoising steps yielding the highest success rate varies from one to four. Even within the same task, different states favor different refinement depths, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser (a.2). Beyond refinement depth, action-to-video attention maps reveal uneven attention across future video regions (shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser (a.3)), motivating selective refinement of regions most relevant to action generation~ yu2026maskwam . Together, these observations motivate adaptive allocation of world refinement computation across both temporal denoising time and spatial future video regions. To this end, we propose Elastic-WAM, which models the demand for world refinement through a unified spatiotemporal field, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser (b). Its total mass governs when to stop world refinement, its temporal profile determines how far to advance each denoising step, and its spatial variation identifies which future video regions to refresh. We parameterize this field with a shared temporal basis and spatial amplitudes that separate global refinement demand from relative regional priorities. We learn this field through three stages of action-grounded supervision, progressively optimizing the temporal profile, relative spatial priorities, and overall refinement demand. At inference, we start with a dense joint denoising step, use the learned field to guide subsequent sparse world refinement, and continue action denoising after world refinement stops. We evaluate Elastic-WAM across in-distribution~ liu2023libero , out-of-distribution~ fei25libero-plus,zhou2025libero , and more complex manipulation simulation benchmarks~ bjorck2025gr00t , as well as a real-world long-horizon tea preparation task. Our results demonstrate state-of-the-art control performance among methods without large-scale embodied pretraining, while reducing inference latency by 32.2 compared with Joint-WAM on RoboCasa-GR1, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser (c). Our contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate adaptive world refinement through a unified spatiotemporal demand field, jointly governing when to stop, how far to advance, and where to refresh future video representations. We develop an action-grounded supervised learning framework and recurrent sparse inference strategy, enabling adaptive refinement with a frozen WAM backbone. We demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, while substantially reducing inference latency. Related Work sec:related_work -Action Models. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have evolved from directly predicting robot actions~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_05,he2026elan4d,xie2026dynamicvla to leveraging future visual predictions to guide action generation~ zhao2025cot,cen2025worldvla,zhang2026dreamvla,wang2026lamp,wang2026openwam . World-Action Models (WAMs) further extend the VLA paradigm by jointly modeling future visual dynamics and robot actions~ ye2026world,bi2026motus,kim2026cosmos,team2026motubrain . To improve inference efficiency, recent approaches exploit partially denoised video representations~ pai2025mimic,ma2026dit4dit,li2026causal , modality-aware step distillation~ akbari2026flash , or compact video experts with sparse latents and asymmetric denoising~ li2026efficient . Other methods eliminate explicit future generation at inference~ yuan2026fast or preserve future conditioning through sparse video--action interactions~ zhao2026faster . Complementary to these approaches, our Elastic-WAM adaptively allocates computation within the recurrent world refinement process of a frozen WAM, across both temporal denoising time and spatial future video regions. Adaptive Denoising. Diffusion sampling has been accelerated through implicit samplers, efficient ODE solvers, and consistency distillation~ song2020denoising,lu2022dpm,luo2023latent , typically using predefined schedules across inputs. Recent approaches further adapt denoising computation to individual inputs: AdaDiff learns sample-specific step budgets~ zhang2025adadiff , while AdaptiveDiffusion skips redundant noise predictions based on intermediate latent changes~ ye2024training . For robotic control, D3P dynamically allocates action denoising steps according to state-dependent action importance~ yu2025d3p , while SANTS learns adaptive stopping and noise progression for WAMs based on downstream action quality~ sun2026sants . While these methods adapt computation along the denoising trajectory, Elastic-WAM jointly governs temporal refinement and spatial future token updates through a unified spatiotemporal refinement field. Adaptive Computation. Spatial redundancy in diffusion transformers has motivated methods that concentrate computation on selected tokens or attention interactions. VSA introduces trainable sparse attention by identifying important token interactions~ zhang2026faster , while VORTA dynamically routes computation among sparse attention patterns~ sun2026vorta . Jenga combines dynamic attention carving with progressive resolution generation~ zhang2026training . Beyond attention sparsification, DyDiT dynamically adjusts computation across denoising timesteps and spatial locations~ zhao2025dynamic , while token-wise feature caching selectively reuses intermediate features across denoising steps~ zou2024accelerating . Elastic-WAM learns to selectively refresh future video queries based on their contribution to downstream action prediction, preserving full logical attention context and coordinating spatial refinement with temporal decisions through a unified field. title: picoEmergencyNet : Attention-Enhanced Ultra-Small Deep Learning Model for Aerial Image Classification in Emergency Monitoring
comment: 6 pages, Appeared in IJCNN2026 C. Kyrkou, "picoEmergencyNet: Attention-Enhanced Ultra-Small Deep Learning Model for Aerial Image Classification in Emergency Monitoring," 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN), Maastricht, Netherlands, 2026, pp. 1-6
summary: Real-time disaster recognition from aerial imagery requires deep learning models that operate under strict memory, compute, and latency constraints. While recent approaches achieve high accuracy, their computational cost limits deployment on resource-constrained UAV platforms. This work introduces picoEmergencyNet, an ultra-lightweight convolutional neural network designed for aerial image disaster classification. The proposed architecture combines depthwise dilated convolutions with efficient channel attention and channel shuffling to enable multi-scale feature extraction at minimal computational cost. picoEmergencyNet has 23k parameters and 7M FLOPs, requiring only 0.1 MB of model storage. Evaluated on the AIDER and AIDERv2 disaster datasets, it achieves up to 96.1% accuracy, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art lightweight models that are orders of magnitude larger. Deployment experiments on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin show that, without hardware-specific optimizations, picoEmergencyNet achieves 258 FPS on GPU and 46 FPS on CPU with a 7x lower activation memory footprint compared to competing models. These results demonstrate that careful architectural specialization, rather than model scaling, enables highly efficient and accurate TinyML-ready disaster recognition for real-time UAV-based emergency monitoring.

Image Classification, UAV (Unmanned Aerial Vehicle), Convolutional Neural Networks, Tiny ML Introduction Advances in technologies such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) 9979171 , have expanded the capabilities of disaster monitoring and response. UAVs provide quick aerial observations in hard-to-reach areas, which may be dangerous for humans to access, and capture high-resolution images, thus enhancing situational awareness over large areas. At the same time, Computer Vision (CV) algorithms based on deep learning techniques can serve as a crucial component for classifying disaster events by analyzing acquired images in real time, either during or in the aftermath of disasters. Consequently, the integration of UAVs with deep learning techniques for disaster recognition holds great promise for further advancements in the field of emergency management 9979171 . In recent times, several efforts have been made towards innovative approaches, which led to the establishment of multiple datasets designed for disaster classification kyrkou2020emergencynet,shianios2024direcnetv2 . Using these datasets multiple networks have been proposed based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs or ConvNets) and lately Vision Transformers (ViTs). ConvNets and ViTs usually differ in their size and complexity, with standard ViTs often being more resource-intensive than ConvNets. Significantly, it should be highlighted that while deeper and more complex models tend to be more accurate, they come at additional cost of increased computational requirements, longer inference times, and heavier workloads. Such constraints become particularly critical in scenarios like emergency and disaster response. title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
full_text: Introduction The 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge The BEHAVIOR Challenge~ behavior_challenge2026,li2024behavior evaluates robot policies on long-horizon household activities in the OmniGibson simulator, built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The 2026 edition doubles the 2025 task set: 100 activities, from turning on a radio to cooking a meal, each with 200 teleoperated demonstrations (20 , 000 episodes, 211M frames or about 1 , 950 hours, in the LeRobot~ cadene2024lerobot format). The robot is the same Galaxea R1Pro: a holonomic base, a 4-joint torso and two 7-DOF arms with parallel grippers, observed through a head camera and two wrist cameras plus proprioception. An episode is a full success if all goal predicates are satisfied, which scores 1. Otherwise its q-score (we also call it Q) is the fraction of satisfied predicates. Scores are averaged over instances and then over tasks. The time limit of an episode is 1.5 the mean duration of the human demonstrations of the task (2 in 2025). The 50 tasks of 2025 are included with the same demonstrations; the other 50 are new. Vision-language-action models Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune a pretrained vision-language model to output robot actions~ brohan2023rt2 . The family~ black2024pi0,pi05_2025 pairs a PaliGemma VLM~ beyer2024paligemma with a smaller ``action expert'' trained by flow matching~ lipman2023flow to generate chunks of continuous actions, optionally co-trained with discrete FAST action tokens~ pertsch2025fast . Many alternatives have appeared since, such as GR00T~ nvidia2025gr00tn1 and, increasingly prominent, MolmoAct2~ fang2026molmoact2 . Yet more than a year after its release (paper in April 2025, code and weights in September 2025~ openpi ), is still widely used as a base for fine-tuning: both top 2025 BEHAVIOR solutions were built on it~ larchenko2025behavior,bai2025comet . We built our 2026 solution on top of our 2025 one, so we kept its -based architecture. For this reason, in parts of this report we call our learned policy simply . LLM agents as robot controllers A second line of work uses large language models to control robots directly: by choosing among learned skills~ ahn2022saycan , writing control code~ liang2023cap , or orchestrating a low-level policy. With frontier models that can use tools for hours, this has become a practical option in simulation. GPT-6 Astra~ openai2026astra , released in September 2026, was strong enough to solve some BEHAVIOR tasks that our learned policy could not, so our final submission routes 14 tasks to an Astra-based agent (Section~ sec:astra ). Our starting point Our 2025 solution~ larchenko2025behavior won the first BEHAVIOR Challenge. It took and changed the following: trainable task embeddings instead of text prompts, correlated noise for flow matching, a learnable mixture of all VLM layers' keys and values for the action expert, a stage-prediction head with voting (``System 2''), a FAST auxiliary loss, several flow samples per VLM forward pass, and correlation-aware inpainting at inference. The 2025 checkpoints were clearly undertrained: the loss was still falling when the deadline came, and four checkpoints split the 50 tasks between them. The LeHome Challenge solution~ larchenko2026lehome of one of our team members was built on top of the 2025 BEHAVIOR solution and introduced several engineering fixes and improvements that we inherit here as well. The 2025 runner-up~ bai2025comet also starts from and studies the effect of image resolution, of the training data and of rejection-sampling fine-tuning. Contributions A recipe for growing a task-conditioned VLA from 50 to 100 tasks without retraining from scratch: semantic stages from skill annotations, similarity-based initialization of new task and stage embeddings, and a 21-dimensional action space matching teleoperation controls (Section~ sec:migration ). Registers, scratch tokens and attention sinks at several levels of a VLA; moving the pretrained SigLIP attention-sink outliers into the registers by parameter surgery on a running training made the attention maps readable (Section~ sec:tokens ). Variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching and a way to choose the number of flow samples from one gradient-noise measurement (Section~ sec:flow ). An evaluation infrastructure that makes cross-cloud rollouts inspectable and reusable through provenance, diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators per GPU faster than real time in aggregate (Section~ sec:eval ). An LLM agent route with GPT-6 Astra for 14 tasks where the learned policy is weak and the agent performed better (Section~ sec:astra ). Code and models. Code: . Checkpoint: . The 2025 checkpoint we start from: . Project page, including evaluation videos and visual examples: . Overall Solution sec:overview What carries over From our 2025 solution we keep the model and most of the serving logic~ larchenko2025behavior : Task embeddings instead of text: each task has a learned embedding, and the prompt is never tokenized. System 2 stages: the model predicts the current stage of the task from the base task token and is conditioned on a stage embedding; at inference the stage is tracked by voting. Correlated flow noise: the flow-matching noise has the covariance ( ), where is the empirical correlation of normalized action chunks, both in training and at inference. KV mixing: each action-expert layer attends to a learnable mixture of the keys and values of all VLM layers. Multi-sample flow matching: the VLM prefix is computed once, and the action expert is run for flow samples (Section~ sec:flow ). FAST auxiliary loss: the VLM also predicts the FAST tokens of the target chunk during training. Correlation-aware inpainting at inference: the actions already committed from the previous chunk anchor the next one, and the action correlations carry the correction over to the free actions. From the LeHome solution~ larchenko2026lehome we take the training side: a weighted multi-dataset loader, corrected state scaling (in 2025 many normalized state values fell outside the range of the state bins and were clipped), loss masking of padded steps at episode ends, and the augmentation set (crop, rotation, color jitter, cutout, camera and state dropout). New in 2026, the frames after the task is complete (the idle tail of each demonstration) are never sampled for training. Model The backbone is that of in its openpi release~ openpi : PaliGemma (SigLIP So400m~ zhai2023siglip and Gemma 2B~ gemma2024 ) as the VLM and a 300M Gemma action expert with adaptive RMS-norm conditioning on the flow time (Figure~ fig:arch ). Images are 224 224 (256 tokens per camera). The prefix holds the image tokens with their SigLIP registers, VLM scratch tokens, the base task token, four task/stage fusion tokens, a continuous state token and 21 quantized state tokens, and in training the FAST tokens of the target chunk. The expert's suffix holds four scratch tokens, the 30 noisy actions and two conditioning tokens. State tokens. embeds each state dimension as one of 256 bin tokens of the language model's embedding table, so ``left shoulder at bin 120'' and ``right wrist at bin 120'' are the same vector, and values outside are clipped. We expanded each of the 21 state tokens to \[ _j = E_ [ (x_j)] + e_j + W\, (x_j), \] so that the same bin maps to a distinct token for each joint, where is a learned per-joint embedding, is a 256-dimensional sine/cosine encoding of the unclipped value, and is a learned projection matrix shared across joints that maps to the token width; and are initialized to zero. In addition to these 21 per-joint tokens, a single continuous state token is a linear projection of the whole unclipped state vector. Task and stage inputs to the action expert. In the expert sees the task only through the VLM's keys and values. We add two tokens at the end of the suffix that carry zero-initialized projections of the task embedding and of the task-stage embedding, a direct conditioning path into the expert. Attention structure. Figure~ fig:mask shows the attention mask. The images, registers, VLM scratch tokens and the base task token form one bidirectional block that cannot see the stage or the state; the stage head reads the output of the base task token, so the stage is predicted from the images and the task alone. The stage and state tokens see that block and each other; the FAST tokens are causal. The action expert's tokens see the whole prefix except the FAST tokens and attend bidirectionally among themselves. Every query can also attend to the sink. Inference. The serving loop is the 2025 one with re-tuned parameters; Appendix~ app:inference lists the changes. Migration from 50 to 100 Tasks sec:migration The 2025 solution served four checkpoints, each fine-tuned on a subset of the 50 tasks. In 2026 one checkpoint serves all 100 tasks. It is warm-started from the 2025 checkpoint that carried the largest share of the 2025 score; a single conversion script maps it to the new task set, stage layout and action space. All parameters added in 2026 are zero-, identity- or small-normal-initialized, so the converted model starts close to the 2025 function. Semantic stages sec:stages In 2025 the System 2 stages were equal slices of each episode in time (5--15 per task), because we did not use the skill annotations. With 20 , 000 annotated demonstrations we could check how well these time slices match the actual steps of the tasks, and they match poorly. On average only 50 of the frames of a time stage belong to its most common annotated step (0.17--0.82 per task); 57 of the 1 , 093 time stages of the 100 tasks have no step that covers more than half of their frames; and the borders of the time stages are no closer to the real step borders than random borders would be. Episode lengths within a task vary by 20 , so in an 11-stage task a fixed time grid can be off by about two stages in either direction. We replaced them with semantic stages built from the annotations (Figure~ fig:stages ): each episode is cut at the frame where the task is complete, and its sequence of annotated skills is aligned to the typical sequence of the task (the medoid); retries and extra steps are assigned to the current step; the steps are grouped into stages at points where the demonstrations agree; parts that demonstrators do in varying order (e.g.\ sorting items) become order-free progress stages; a few rules then adjust the grouping: a grasp and a press-type action (press, switch, toggle) are never in the same stage, so that the gripper rule (Appendix~ app:inference ) can tell a missed grasp from a press; similar-looking states of the same appliance are kept in separate stages; repeated steps in a row become one stage; very short stages are merged into a neighbour unless they are a distinct final action. The result has 413 stages (2--9 per task) instead of 1 , 093 time stages. Every label is regenerated from the dataset annotations by deterministic scripts. Warm-starting new tasks and stages Tasks. The 50 tasks of 2025 keep their trained embeddings. We could initialize the 50 new ones randomly, but many new tasks are similar to old ones, so instead each new task starts from a weighted average of the embeddings of 1--5 similar 2025 tasks (most have three), with weights by rank. The average is rescaled to the average norm of its sources, because averaging makes vectors shorter. title: Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
summary: Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies are meant to remember what happened. Many of them, however, fill memory by time: they sample frames uniformly across the episode and stamp each frame with its time step. Because time passes even when nothing happens, such a memory may not tell waiting from working. We show that it does not. On the counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the robot briefly pause or fidget its wrist. Such a null event changes nothing the task depends on, yet a released memory VLA counts the interval as work done and stops early. We call this failure phantom progress. It cuts success from 47 to 16 of 50 on one task and from 44 to 10 on the other. When the same frames are withheld from memory, success returns, so the cause lies in memory rather than in the interruption itself. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut: because demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, elapsed time predicts progress. Indeed, rescaling the time stamps alone makes the policy stop early when the clock runs fast and repeat when it runs slow. Surprisingly, removing the time encoding does not cure the failure, because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of the time-sampled memory. Across RoboMME's released designs, vulnerability follows how memory is indexed. Of the fixes the diagnosis suggests, training with injected pauses does not remove the failure and impairs counting, whereas indexing memory by events recovers half or more of the loss without retraining. A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks.

A memory meant to remember what happened should count events rather than clock ticks. Introduction sec:intro Many manipulation tasks cannot be solved from the current observation alone. A robot asked to pick up a cube three times and then press a button sees much the same scene before its second pick as before its third, so it has to remember how many picks it has made. Memory-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies address this by conditioning each action on a memory of the episode so far~ shi2026memoryvla,sridhar2026memer,torne2026mem,dai2026robomme . A simple and widely used way to fill such a memory is by time: the policy samples past frames uniformly over the episode and stamps each frame with its time step. This design covers the whole episode at a fixed cost, and on RoboMME~ dai2026robomme , a benchmark built to test memory, the strongest released policy uses exactly this design. However, time passes even when nothing happens. Real robots often wait for a slow planner, for an operator who has paused them, or for a safety monitor to clear. They also hesitate, or reach for an object and come back empty-handed. We call such an interval a null event. It takes time, and the robot may even move, yet nothing the task depends on changes. A memory that records what happened should therefore pass over a null event as if it had not occurred. A memory filled by time cannot do so, because the interval receives its share of sampled frames and time stamps like any other stretch of the episode. This raises a simple question: Can a memory filled by time tell waiting from working? We find that it cannot ( ). On the two counting tasks of RoboMME, we make the released policy pause twice for 5 seconds, or roll its wrist back and forth for as long. Success falls from 47 to 16 of 50 on PickXtimes and from 44 to 10 on SwingXtimes. Almost every failure is an early stop, in which the policy presses the button before it has made the required number of repetitions. The robot thus perceives progress that never happened. We call this failure phantom progress. One might suspect that the interruption itself disturbs the robot, for instance by leaving its arm in an unusual pose. We therefore repeat each event with its frames withheld from memory. The robot pauses or fidgets exactly as before, but its memory never sees the interval, and success returns to within three episodes of the baseline. The failure therefore lies in what the policy remembers. Why would a policy mistake waiting for working? We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut. Demonstrations proceed at a steady pace, so elapsed time alone predicts how many repetitions are done 89 and 80 of the time on the two tasks, and over 92 on regular demonstrations from two real teleoperation datasets. Since demonstrations contain almost no idle stretches, imitation learning never penalises a policy for reading progress from time. If the policy indeed reads progress from time, rescaling the time stamps alone should shift its failures in a predictable direction. It does: with no null event and the frames unchanged, a faster clock makes the policy stop early, and a slower one makes it repeat ( ). The obvious remedy is then to remove the time encoding. Surprisingly, a policy trained from scratch without it still fails under pauses (21 and 14 of 50), because the frames of a null event still occupy slots of a memory sampled by time ( ). The shortcut thus lies in how memory is indexed, and the time stamps are only one of its carriers. Consistently, among RoboMME's released designs, every memory indexed by time collapses under null events, a memory that selects tokens by pixel change is hurt less by pauses than by fidgets, and memories indexed by sub-goals withstand both null events on PickXtimes ( ). The diagnosis also suggests where to fix the failure. Training with injected pauses changes the data but keeps the index, so at best it can teach the policy to discount the null events that we know how to synthesise. It does not even achieve this: pause augmentation does not remove the failure, and it impairs counting when no null event occurs. Changing the index should work instead. Indexing memory by events collapses every stretch in which the world returns to a state it was already in. Applied at test time without retraining, it recovers half or more of the lost success under pauses, fidgets and air-grasps alike ( ). We summarize our contributions as follows: Phantom progress. Brief null events make memory VLAs that fill memory by time stop early, and the damage passes through memory alone. Comparing visible with hidden null events, together with rescaling the time stamps, gives a protocol for testing whether any memory policy tracks events or elapsed time ( ). A shortcut in the index. We trace the failure to a temporal shortcut that lives in how memory is indexed, so that removing the time stamps does not remove it, and we show that vulnerability follows the index across RoboMME's released designs ( ). Fixes suggested by the diagnosis. Pause augmentation does not remove the failure, whereas indexing memory by events recovers much of the loss without retraining ( ). Related Work sec:related Memory in robot policies. Most VLA policies act on the current observation or a short window~ black2025pi0,black2025pi05,zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion . A growing line adds memory: history-aware transformers~ guhur2022hiveformer,li2024roboflamingo,wu2024gr1,koo2026hamlet , perceptual memory banks~ shi2026memoryvla,fang2025sam2act , keyframe and event selection~ sridhar2026memer,mark2026bpp,zeng2026kemo,yang2026eventvla , recurrent and test-time-training memories~ bulatov2022rmt,sun2025ttt,liu2026t2mem , and mixed video--language memory~ torne2026mem . RoboMME~ dai2026robomme standardises their evaluation and releases the MME-VLA family we study, and MIKASA-Robo~ cherepanov2025mikasa and MemoryBench~ fang2025sam2act are related suites. Such benchmarks ask which memory scores highest. A smaller set of works asks what memory actually does. History can be encoded yet barely used~ liao2026present , and long or uncurated histories invite spurious correlations~ mark2026bpp,wu2026imprint,torne2025pasttoken . These works treat the problem as a shift in the distribution of histories and remedy it by choosing which frames to keep. We instead identify one specific correlate, elapsed time, show by intervention that the policy reads it, and find that selecting memory content by appearance does not remove it. Closest to us, AGM~ gao2026agm shows that memories logging attempted actions as progress turn a failed grasp into a persistent error, and RoboMME-Interference~ rathi2026interference shows that unrelated sessions crowd frame-sampled memories. Concurrent event-driven keyframe memories~ zeng2026kemo,yang2026eventvla report that selecting frames by events beats uniform sampling. Our analysis explains why such memories should resist null events, and our event index ( ) is a minimal intervention that tests this account rather than a new architecture. Shortcuts, time, and position. Shortcut learning~ geirhos2020shortcut is well documented in imitation learning, as causal confusion~ dehaan2019causal and copycat behaviour of history-conditioned policies~ wen2020copycat,chuang2022residual . Elapsed time is a special case: it is legitimately part of the state under time limits~ pardo2018time , many controllers are driven by a phase variable~ ijspeert2013dmp,peng2018deepmimic , and progress estimators are tempted by temporal position, which is why GVL shuffles frames~ ma2025gvl . In sequence models, positional encodings shape counting and length generalisation~ press2022alibi,anil2022length,kazemnejad2023nope,ruoss2023randomized , and video moment-retrieval models can answer from the temporal position of a moment rather than the video content~ otani2020uncovering,yuan2021closer . We show that in memory VLAs the time position becomes a substitute for content, and that removing the explicit encoding does not remove it. Events and redundancy in video memory. Video models compress long inputs by merging redundant frames or tokens~ bolya2023tome,song2024moviechat,he2024malmm , and event segmentation~ zacks2007event,shou2021gebd,fountas2025emllm groups frames into meaningful units. Such methods judge redundancy by appearance. A null event need not look redundant: a fidgeting wrist changes every frame. Our event-indexed memory instead uses whether the world returns to a previous state, in the spirit of loop closure in SLAM~ cadena2016slam . Robustness of robot policies. title: RF3DGS: Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting with Self-Priors
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Joint first authors: Qiang Wen, Guotao Meng, and Junhong Ruan
summary: 3D reflection removal is crucial in applications demanding high-fidelity visualization, such as museum exhibitions. In this work, we propose Reflection-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting (RF3DGS), a novel method for superior reflection removal. RF3DGS exclusively leverages a widely-adopted photometric prior for reflection removal: that the minimum pixel intensity across multi-view images corresponding to the same 3D point strongly correlates with reflection-free information. However, generalizing this principle to a 3D Gaussian Splatting within a multi-view context is non-trivial. To address this, RF3DGS first optimizes a vanilla 3DGS model using a geometric prior to estimate a coarse, reflection-free depth map for each view. Leveraging these depth maps and photometric prior, a 3D warping process aggregates reflection-free information from auxiliary views to construct a clean transmission pseudo-label for a given reference view. This pseudo-label provides a robust self-supervised signal for optimization. We further introduce an Adaptive Twin Rendering (ATR) loss to synergistically utilize this pseudo-label while preserving high-frequency details from the original, reflection-degraded images. By adeptly fusing these internal 3D self-priors with the ATR loss, RF3DGS demonstrates state-of-the-art reflection removal performance across both synthetic and real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we establish the first 3D reflection removal benchmark, based on the Unity rendering engine, for rigorous quantitative evaluation.

Introduction sec:intro Capturing photos with undesirable reflections is common in daily scenarios, such as exhibitions shown in Fig.~ fig: teaser . Reflection removal seeks to restore clean transmission for better visual quality and improved downstream computer vision performance~ redmon2016you . However, removing reflections in real-world scenarios remains ill-posed. Learning-based methods improve robustness with additional priors, e.g., edge maps~ fan2017generic , polarization~ lei2020polarized , textual prompts~ zhong2024language, ldiffer_hong , and flash/no-flash cues~ lei2023robust . Due to limited scene coverage in current datasets~ zhang2018single, zhu2024revisiting, wan2017benchmarking, li2020single, lei2020polarized, niklaus2021learned, wang2022background, Liu_CVPR_2020 , such methods still suffer from domain gap and often fail under strong reflections or non-ideal guidance. Multi-frame methods~ guo2014robust, Xue2015ObstructionFree, gai2011blind, li2013exploiting, alayrac2019visual, chugunov2024neural can aggregate clean information across frames, yet priors from limited neighbors (e.g., optical flow) remain too weak for strong reflections or significant motions~ li2013exploiting, chugunov2024neural . Thanks to progress in 3D neural scene representations~ mildenhall2020nerf, kerbl3Dgaussians , 3D reflection removal methods~ Guo_2022_CVPR, flash_splat, wang2024dc, gao2024planar, zhu2022neural show strong robustness via multi-view consistency and crafted assumptions. Both NeRF-based (e.g., TNeRF~ zhu2022neural , NeRFReN~ Guo_2022_CVPR ) and 3DGS-based methods (e.g., DC-Gaussian~ wang2024dc , Flash-Splat~ flash_splat ) perform well. However, NeRFReN’s long training and rendering times hinder practicality, while pixel-wise optimization limits global perceptual quality. Flash-Splat exploits real-time 3DGS rendering~ kerbl3Dgaussians , but its reliance on flash/no-flash cues~ lei2023robust, xia2021deep, xia2021dark in RAW images complicates capture and SfM; these cues also weaken as camera–scene distance grows. To inherit the robustness and overcome the weaknesses of current 3D reflection removal methods, we propose a novel reflection-free 3DGS method for the 3D reflection removal task. The proposed method simplifies the capture process by requiring only a monocular sRGB video, easily obtained with any mobile phone or DSLR camera, without relying on specialized photography techniques such as capturing flash or no-flash RAW images~ flash_splat . Inspired by Li~ ~ li2013exploiting , we leverage the Photometric Prior in real-world reflection scenarios: for a given 3D scene point, the minimum intensity value across all captured views strongly corresponds to reflection-free information. Since pixel values from the captured views must be accurately projected back into 3D space, obtaining precise depth maps is crucial to effectively apply the photometric prior. Benefiting from explicit depth estimation in 3DGS, we can efficiently generate depth maps for each captured view by optimizing a vanilla 3DGS model under reflection conditions. To ensure the depth maps contain as pure reflection-free depth information as possible, we incorporate a Geometric Prior—also used by NeRFReN~ Guo_2022_CVPR —within 3DGS, which encourages smoothness in the rendered depth maps. This geometric prior assumes that the depth map of the transmitted component should be locally smoother than that of the reflection-degraded one. Utilizing these refined depth maps, we project all captured views back into the 3D space and apply the photometric prior, then re-render each view with preliminary clean transmission information. Due to the flaws of depth maps and imperfect projections, current reflection-free views still have inevitable artifacts, as shown in Fig.~ fig: 3D_warp . Directly optimizing the 3DGS on them leads to poor 3D consistency and color distortion. To address this issue, the proposed method goes into the comprehensive optimization where original captured views and preliminary reflection-free views are jointly treated as supervision during 3DGS optimization. We propose an Adaptive Twin Rending (ATR) loss to achieve this joint supervision, encouraging the 3DGS model to effectively capture the clean transmission information from preliminary reflection-free views and maintain the original 3D consistency for a reflection-degraded scene. Furthermore, recognizing that existing benchmarks provide limited scene diversity—for example, TNeRF~ zhu2022neural includes only four scenes—for quantitatively evaluating 3D reflection removal methods, we introduce a comprehensive 3D reflection removal benchmark aimed at significantly enhancing evaluation diversity. Since capturing videos with and without reflections along the exact same camera trajectory is challenging, we leverage the precise camera control capabilities of the modern rendering engine Unity~ haas2014history to construct our benchmark. To guarantee the diversity of our benchmark, we build 3D scenes with different settings (background reflection scenes, glass thickness, transparency and reflection strength), resulting in 45 cases for evaluation. Besides, we additionally collect real-world cases for qualitative evaluation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms previous works on the proposed benchmark and across various real-world scenarios. This strong robustness and simplicity of our method indicate its potential for practical applications. title: Marrying Capacity and Precision for Efficient 2D Gaussian Image Representation
summary: 2D Gaussian representations provide an explicit and efficient way to represent images, but their rate-distortion performance under limited budgets depends critically on how Gaussian capacity and parameter precision are allocated. Existing methods typically optimize these two resources separately, overlooking content-dependent capacity demands and heterogeneous quantization sensitivity. We present CP-GS, a capacity-precision coupled Gaussian splatting framework for budget-aware 2D Gaussian image representation that jointly optimizes capacity allocation and attribute precision under a shared rate constraint. CP-GS first constructs a content-adaptive Gaussian representation by dynamically reallocating a fixed Gaussian budget from redundant regions to areas with higher representation demand. It then introduces hierarchical distortion-aware representation quantization, using efficient rendering-based calibration to allocate precision across Gaussian attributes and further refine it within heterogeneous attribute groups. Finally, it jointly optimizes Gaussian capacity and attribute precision by constructing candidate representations with different Gaussian counts and precision configurations and selecting operating points according to decoded distortion and actual serialized size. Experiments on DIV2K and Kodak show that CP-GS achieves improved rate-distortion performance over representative 2D Gaussian and implicit neural representations across a range of budgets, while maintaining a fixed overall representation budget and low optimization cost. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly optimizing spatial capacity and parameter precision for compact Gaussian image representation.
