Introduction Efficient image representation aims to encode visual content compactly while preserving the information necessary for faithful reconstruction and downstream processing~ zhang20252dmamba, kao2025bridging . Such representations serve as a fundamental building block for a wide range of visual tasks, including image reconstruction~ tian2025degradation , super-resolution~ chen2021learning , restoration~ jiang2025survey , editing~ ye2026imgedit , and generation~ xiao2025omnigen . Building on the success of Gaussian primitives as an explicit representation for 3D scenes, 2D Gaussian splatting has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for image representation. It models visual content with a finite set of learnable anisotropic Gaussian primitives rather than dense pixels or implicit neural fields~ hu2025gaussiansr . Its explicit and differentiable formulation enables compact parameterization, efficient rendering, and flexible primitive-level manipulation, making it particularly attractive for efficient image representation. However, representation efficiency critically depends on how the model allocates Gaussian capacity and parameter precision under a constraint budget. Existing approaches improve the efficiency of 2D Gaussian image representation primarily along two separate dimensions: representation capacity and parameter precision. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:intro (a), representation-oriented methods~ zhang2024gaussianimage,li2026gaussianimagepp , such as Image-GS~ zhang2025image , focus on constructing and optimizing Gaussian primitives to match image content and reconstruction demands better. In parallel, Gaussian compression methods~ liang2025structure,chen2026pcgs reduce storage costs through uniform or manually designed quantization schemes, assigning predefined precisions to position, geometry, and color attributes. However, representation capacity and attribute precision are typically optimized separately, with the Gaussian capacity determined before attribute quantization. This decoupled treatment overlooks the fact that both resources compete for the same coding budget. Under a fixed rate, a representation may favor either more low-precision Gaussians for broader spatial coverage or fewer high-precision Gaussians for more faithful per-primitive encoding. Therefore, the preferred capacity and precision are inherently interdependent and should be jointly optimized rather than determined in isolation. Figure~ fig:intro (b) highlights three key observations that motivate CP-GS. First, Gaussian capacity may not match content demand. Redundant Gaussians can accumulate in over-represented regions, while high-residual regions remain under-represented. This suggests that a fixed Gaussian budget should remain reallocatable based on content demand. Second, Gaussian attributes exhibit heterogeneous quantization sensitivity. Their sensitivity varies across attributes and within attributes, making uniform precision inefficient and motivating hierarchical distortion-aware quantization without exhaustive search. Third, capacity and precision are coupled under a shared budget. Increasing Gaussian capacity improves spatial coverage but reduces precision available to each primitive, whereas higher precision improves attribute fidelity at the cost of fewer Gaussians. This inherent trade-off motivates jointly optimizing capacity and precision in a unified rate-distortion space. Motivated by these observations, we propose CP-GS, a Capacity-Precision coupled Gaussian Splatting framework for budget-aware 2D Gaussian image representation. CP-GS first constructs a content-adaptive representation by reallocating a fixed Gaussian budget from redundant primitives to high-demand regions. It then performs hierarchical distortion-aware quantization to allocate precision according to heterogeneous quantization sensitivity at both the attribute and intra-attribute levels. Finally, CP-GS jointly optimizes Gaussian capacity and attribute precision as competing representation resources under a shared budget, adaptively balancing spatial coverage and per-primitive fidelity. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:intro (c), CP-GS therefore adapts both the spatial distribution and precision of Gaussian primitives to image content and representation budget. Extensive experiments on DIV2K and Kodak demonstrate that CP-GS achieves improved rate-distortion performance across a wide range of representation budgets. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We develop a content-adaptive 2D Gaussian representation that reallocates a fixed Gaussian budget from redundant primitives to high-demand regions, improving capacity utilization without increasing the initial primitive budget. We introduce hierarchical distortion-aware representation quantization that models heterogeneous quantization sensitivity at both the attribute and intra-attribute levels, enabling efficient mixed-precision allocation without exhaustive search. We propose capacity-precision coupled optimization that jointly optimizes Gaussian capacity and attribute precision as competing representation resources, enabling adaptive trade-offs between spatial coverage and per-primitive fidelity under a shared budget. Related Work Explicit 2D Gaussian representations have recently emerged as an efficient alternative to INR-based image codecs, such as SIREN~ sitzmann2020implicit and COIN~ dupont2021coin . Gaussian-based methods represent images with position, covariance, and color parameters, and support fast differentiable rasterization~ zhang2024gaussianimage . Subsequent works have extended this paradigm along two main directions: continuous and arbitrary-scale signal representation~ hu2025gaussiansr,peng2025continuoussr , and compact or structured encoding~ pan2026sgi . Collectively, these works demonstrate that 2D Gaussians provide an explicit and highly adaptable representation space. Our work builds on this perspective but focuses on how limited representation resources should be distributed between Gaussian capacity and parameter precision. A central problem in 2D Gaussian image representation is how to allocate a finite number of primitives according to spatially varying image complexity. Image-GS~ zhang2025image performs content-adaptive allocation by progressively placing anisotropic Gaussians according to image content. GaussianImage++~ li2026gaussianimagepp uses distortion-driven densification to allocate primitives according to signal intensity. Instant GaussianImage~ zeng2025instant predicts Gaussian parameters in a feed-forward manner, enabling self-adaptive representation without per-image optimization. LocoADC~ chen2026locoadc exploits locality in both image and Gaussian spaces through region-wise densification and similarity-driven merging. From a frequency-domain perspective, Spectrum-Adaptive Distribution~ wan2025spectrum distributes Gaussians according to spectral characteristics, while GPSToken~ zhang2026gpstoken uses entropy-driven partitioning to achieve non-uniform tokenization. At the budget level, SPARE-GS~ chen2026sparegs formulates structural evolution as a global budget-constrained optimization problem. In the 3DGS domain, GDAGS~ zhou2026gdags introduces gradient-direction-aware density control. Collectively, these methods establish adaptive density control as an effective mechanism for improving spatial capacity utilization. However, they primarily determine where primitives should be created, retained, merged, or removed, while attribute precision is typically fixed or optimized separately. Gaussian compression reduces representation cost through quantization, pruning, and entropy coding of primitive attributes. Structure-Guided Allocation~ liang2025structure couples image structure with adaptive bitwidth quantization, while CGVQ~ cheng2026cgvq applies K-means-guided codebook quantization. In the 3DGS domain, RDO-Gaussian~ wang2024rdogaussian formulates end-to-end rate-distortion optimized compression with dynamic pruning and entropy-constrained quantization. CAT-3DGS~ zhan2025cat3dgs employs context-adaptive triplane autoregressive coding to capture inter- and intra-primitive correlations. CSGaussian~ tseng2026csgaussian combines compression and segmentation using an INR-based hyperprior, while HAC~ chen2024hac introduces hash-grid-assisted context for entropy coding. PCGS~ chen2026pcgs studies progressive compression for scalable decoding, and HilComp~ huang2025hilcomp uses Hilbert curve-based balanced clustering for compact 3D Gaussian representation. Collectively, these studies show that Gaussian attributes have heterogeneous coding requirements and that representation structure affects rate-distortion behavior. However, existing methods typically optimize precision under a fixed Gaussian capacity or treat capacity and precision as sequentially optimized resources. In contrast, CP-GS treats adaptive Gaussian modeling as one dimension of representation allocation and jointly optimizes attribute precision and Gaussian capacity under a shared budget. title: FastWild-GS: Minutes-Scale In-the-Wild Gaussian Splatting via Compact Per-Image Appearance Adaptation
summary: Internet photos of a scene differ in exposure, illumination and transient objects such as passers-by, so one set of Gaussian colours cannot explain all photos (the in-the-wild setting). Recent in-the-wild Gaussian Splatting methods mostly report hours of per-scene optimization. We present FastWild-GS, which describes each photo by a 128-dimensional Photo Appearance Token and a per-channel transform, a scale and an offset applied to the rendered image (six parameters); a small MLP predicts the colour of each Gaussian from this token and a per-Gaussian feature, replacing the spherical-harmonics colour. The same transform is applied to the renders that score Gaussians for densification and pruning, so appearance differences between photos are not counted as reconstruction error. On PhotoTourism, FastWild-GS trains in 8.8 minutes per scene with the lowest LPIPS among the compared methods, 23x faster than AsymGS, the next best in LPIPS. On NeRF-OSR, it has the best average PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS among the compared methods in 9.7 minutes per scene.

Introduction sec:intro In-the-wild novel-view synthesis reconstructs a scene from Internet photo collections~ snavely2006photo , taken by different cameras at different times of day and seasons: the same surface differs in brightness and colour across images, and transient objects appear in only some of them. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussian explains all images with one shared scene and averages these differences. In-the-wild methods add image-specific appearance models~ martinbrualla2021nerfw,kulhanek2024wildgaussians , but recent ones mostly report hours of per-scene optimization ( ). Accelerated 3DGS training reaches minutes~ ren2026fastgs,chen2025dashgaussian,hanson2025speedy , but assumes captures with consistent appearance. We introduce , which trains an in-the-wild scene in minutes ( ). Each photo is described by a Photo Appearance Token (PAT) and a per-image channel transform, a per-channel scale and offset applied to the rendered image. A small MLP, the PAT Decoder, predicts the colour of each Gaussian from the PAT and a per-Gaussian feature, replacing the spherical-harmonics colour ( ). The densification and pruning adopted from FastGS~ ren2026fastgs score Gaussians by the error between renders and photos; on photo collections this error is also high where only exposure or colour differs, so Gaussians can be added on surfaces that are already reconstructed. We therefore apply the per-image transform to the scoring renders ( ). A growth schedule keeps the number of Gaussians low early in training, which keeps early iterations cheap ( ). For a held-out photo, the scene stays fixed and only the appearance parameters of that photo are fitted on the left half of the image; the right half is evaluated ( ). On PhotoTourism~ martinbrualla2021nerfw , has the lowest LPIPS among the compared methods and trains faster than the next best, AsymGS~ asymgs ( ). Contributions. A compact per-image appearance module for in-the-wild Gaussian Splatting: a Photo Appearance Token per image, a shared PAT Decoder and a channel transform. Colour-matched densification scoring: the same transform is applied to the renders that drive densification and pruning, without additional renders. Evidence that the appearance module is not tied to one training method: it improves PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS on six public 3DGS backbones ( ). Related Work sec:related 3D Gaussian Splatting and training acceleration. Neural radiance fields~ mildenhall2021nerf established optimization-based novel-view synthesis from posed photographs, and multiresolution hash encoding~ muller2022instantngp cut their training cost. 3DGS~ kerbl2023gaussian represents a scene with optimized anisotropic Gaussian primitives and enables fast rasterized rendering. FastGS~ ren2026fastgs accelerates 3DGS with multi-view consistent densification and pruning; we adopt these two steps and its rasterizer. DashGaussian~ chen2025dashgaussian schedules rendering resolution together with the primitive count so that the count stays low early in training, as our growth schedule does. Speedy-Splat~ hanson2025speedy prunes aggressively right before opacity resets and at fixed intervals after densification; our four early pruning steps lie just before its first four pruning positions. Turbo-GS~ dhiman2026turbo grows the count along a budget curve, efficient density control~ edc2024 lowers the split threshold in steps, AdpSplit~ adpsplit2026 speeds up FastGS further at equal count, and SAD-GS~ lyu2026sadgs raises the count and shortens training to 3k iterations. A complementary line of work makes the scene representation itself compact by pruning primitives~ lee2024compact,fan2024lightgaussian,liu2025maskgaussian ; the compactness studied in this paper instead concerns the image-specific appearance state. All of these methods are evaluated on static scenes, where the densification error of a render reflects geometry; on photo collections it also reflects the appearance of each photo, which is what our colour-matched scoring addresses. In-the-wild appearance modeling. NeRF-W~ martinbrualla2021nerfw introduced the standard PhotoTourism setting, per-image appearance embeddings and the protocol of fitting the test-image embedding on one half of the image and evaluating on the other. Subsequent NeRF-based methods refine the same setting with hallucinated appearance transfer and cross-ray feature aggregation~ chen2022hanerf,yang2023crnerf . Gaussian Splatting methods such as Wild-GS~ xu2024wildgs , GS-W~ zhang2024gsw and WildGaussians~ kulhanek2024wildgaussians use image-conditioned, transformation-based or multi-scale mechanisms to model appearance variation. WildGaussians conditions appearance on a per-image code together with a per-Gaussian feature and a small colour MLP; adopts this conditioning interface. WilLaGS~ willags conditions a tri-plane appearance field on a per-image latent code, whereas the appearance of a photo in is a single vector and a channel transform. Per-image affine colour corrections are used by Splatfacto-W~ nerfstudio2023splatfactow and by hierarchical 3DGS~ kerbl2024hierarchical ; we apply such a transform both in training and in densification scoring. Recent robust in-the-wild 3DGS variants. Recent work explores richer appearance-conditioned or robustness-oriented Gaussian models, including SWAG~ dahmani2024swag , NexusSplats~ nexussplats , SpotLessSplats~ sabour2024spotlesssplats , AsymGS~ asymgs and ForestSplats~ forestsplats . RobustSplat~ fu2025robustsplat delays densification in the wild to avoid fitting transients, and RobustSplat++~ robustsplatpp2025 uses an appearance MLP and the same half-image test protocol on a plain 3DGS backbone. These methods target stronger appearance modeling or distractor handling; we focus on per-scene optimization time. Other variants address efficiency: WL-GS~ wang2025wlgs reduces memory use for resource-limited hardware, Look at the Sky~ wang2025lookatthesky uses pseudo transient masks from a pretrained segmentation network and separate sky and building appearance embeddings for faster convergence, and 3DGS-W~ chen2026threedgsw looks up transient objects in a 2D dense grid instead of storing them in the Gaussian attributes. Image-level and multi-scale appearance models. title: From Video Frames to Robot Meta-Frames: A Unified Latent Interface for World Action Models
summary: Pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) offer a powerful foundation for World Action Models (WAMs), which jointly predict robot actions and future observations. Building such models requires injecting low-dimensional robot signals (e.g. proprioception, actions, and values) into a latent space shaped by natural videos, and a key design choice is the interface through which these signals enter: existing schemes treat it as a formatting detail, spending a separate latent frame on each signal or bolting on dedicated encoders and decoders. We argue that signal injection is instead a distribution-alignment problem: how well a representation matches the prior of the pretrained VDMs during denoising. Using the relative reconstruction error of a frozen VDM denoiser as a probe, we find that conventional spatial encodings sit far off this prior, whereas frequency-domain packing yields latents that the denoiser corrects far less. Motivated by this diagnostic result, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all robot signals into a single unified meta-frame: each signal is assigned to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band and lifted to the spatial latent by an inverse DCT, yielding a decodable interface aligned with the pretrained VDM prior without any added module or architectural change. A fixed band layout together with slot-aware routing lets the same meta-frame support policy, world-model, and value prediction over a shared set of robot variables. On RoboCasa, MetaWAM reaches 68.9% success while collapsing the per-signal frames into one and cutting inference latency by 39%, and attains 85.0% success on three real-world Franka tasks. Code and models are available at https://github.com/showlab/MetaWAM

Introduction Vision-Language-Action models have become a powerful paradigm for generalist robot control, yet they learn reactive observation-to-action mappings without modeling how the world evolves under their actions~ wang2026world . World Action Models (WAMs) close this gap by adapting pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs), which carry strong spatiotemporal priors over scene dynamics, to predict actions and future observations jointly. Existing WAMs differ mainly in how they couple world prediction and control. Cascaded WAMs use the video model as a learned simulator and recover actions through a separate inverse-dynamics model or policy~ unipi2023, genie2024, liu2026world , while Joint WAMs let one generative backbone emit actions, future observations, and values within a single denoising process~ cosmospolicy2026,dreamzero2026 . Across these designs, a key interface is often treated as a formatting detail: how low-dimensional robot variables, such as proprioception, actions, task type, and values, should enter a latent space shaped by natural-video statistics. This raises the question: how should structured robot signals be represented so that a pretrained VDM treats them as in-distribution during denoising? A straightforward solution injects each robot signal as its own video-like latent frame, either by spatially tiling the raw signal across the frame~ cosmospolicy2026 or by rendering it into an image and re-encoding it through the pretrained VAE~ bu2025agibot ; both preserve backbone compatibility but inflate the sequence length and the quadratic attention cost it incurs. Other designs attach dedicated action encoders or decoders~ dreamzero2026 , improving action modeling at the cost of modifying the pretrained backbone. We view signal injection as a distribution-alignment problem: a useful representation must remain compatible with the VDM prior seen by the pretrained denoiser. As previewed in Fig.~ fig:teaser (b), frequency-domain encoding produces latents that the frozen denoiser corrects far less than spatial encodings. To examine this design space, we run diagnostic experiments that trace candidate injections through VDM denoising, covering both single-signal injection and multi-signal packing, and measure how strongly a frozen denoiser corrects the injected latent across noise levels. These experiments show that the arrangement of robot signals in latent space measurably affects the denoiser: frequency-domain packing yields latents it corrects far less than spatial tiling or discontinuous canvas layouts. Compactness alone is therefore insufficient; an effective interface must be distribution-aware. Motivated by these findings, we propose MetaWAM, which folds all heterogeneous robot signals into a single unified meta-frame (Fig.~ fig:teaser (a)). Rather than allocating a latent frame to each signal, MetaWAM assigns every signal, including current and future proprioception, action chunks, task type, and value, to a disjoint frequency-domain channel band within one frame, and lifts the packed coefficients to the spatial latent via an analytical inverse DCT. This produces smooth latent patterns well aligned with the pretrained denoiser, while a single meta-frame becomes a multiplexed carrier for many low-dimensional signals. The design requires no additional action encoder, learned decoder, or modification to the denoising architecture, and recovers each signal analytically at readout. We instantiate MetaWAM on a Cosmos-Predict2 backbone and evaluate it on RoboCasa, LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and three real-world Franka tabletop tasks. MetaWAM exceeds the RoboCasa frame-injection baseline while collapsing multiple robot-signal frames into one. Our contributions are: (1) we recast robot-signal injection as a distribution-aware latent-interface problem for Joint WAMs; (2) we provide diagnostic evidence that frequency-domain packing aligns better with a pretrained VDM prior than spatial signal encodings; and (3) we introduce a unified frequency-domain meta-frame that carries all robot signals in a single decoder-free latent frame without architectural changes. Related Work World Action Models. World Action Models (WAMs) recast robot control as generative modeling over future states and actions~ wang2026world . Cascaded WAMs generate or represent future observations first and then recover actions through a separate policy or inverse-dynamics model~ unipi2023, genie2024,jang2025dreamgen . Joint WAMs instead couple action and future-state prediction inside one backbone. Cosmos Policy~ cosmospolicy2026 injects actions, proprioception, future states, and values as additional latent frames, preserving the pretrained video architecture; DreamZero~ dreamzero2026 uses dedicated action encoders and decoders around a video backbone; and UWM/UVA~ uwm2025,uva2025 decouple video and action diffusion schedules to enable mixed robot and video training. Recent efficiency-oriented WAMs reduce inference cost by changing what is denoised or attended to, such as removing future-frame generation at test time~ fastwam2026 or emphasizing action-centered decoding~ ye2026gigaworld . MetaWAM is orthogonal to these directions: it keeps the pretrained denoising architecture intact but changes how robot signals are represented inside the latent sequence. Rather than treating signal injection as a formatting choice, we study its compatibility with the pretrained VDM prior and introduce a distribution-aware interface. Latent signal representations. A broad line of work studies how robot or agent signals should be encoded into compact latent forms. Learned schemes include VQ-VAE latent action codes derived from visual dynamics~ lapa2024,moto2024 , world-model-grounded latent actions~ lawm2025 , highly compressed discrete action chunks~ vqace2024 , and modality-specific latent positions for proprioception, actions, and future tokens~ flare2025 . Transform-based schemes exploit frequency structure: FAST~ fast2025 applies 1D DCT to robot action sequences, while wavelet tokenizers~ wavelettokenizer2024 , FA-VAE~ favae2025 , and DocPedia~ docpedia2024 use frequency-domain representations for visual or document modeling. MetaWAM differs in target and mechanism: it uses channel-wise 2D DCT bands to pack heterogeneous robot signals directly into the latent space of a pretrained VDM, lifts them back to the spatial domain by analytical iDCT, and recovers them without a learned decoder. Motivating Analysis sec:motivating_analysis What kind of robot-signal injection does a pretrained VDM actually accept? We probe candidate injections by a single criterion, VDM-prior compatibility, defined by the relative reconstruction error of a frozen Cosmos-Predict2 denoiser~ cosmoswfm2025 on the injected latent: the denoising residual is normalized by the magnitude of the clean latent. Reference latents are drawn from real RoboCasa observations, and we evaluate this error across noise levels . An in-distribution latent needs only small relative corrections; a large residual marks it as off-prior. Fig.~ fig:motivation and Tab.~ tab:vdm_prior_compat summarize the schemes and results. Single-signal injection. We isolate a single signal and compare the three schemes in Fig.~ fig:motivation (a--c): Spatial Duplication (the Cosmos Policy~ cosmospolicy2026 strategy), VAE Encoding (canvas overlay through the VAE~ bu2025agibot ), and DCT Encoding (raw DCT coefficients written into a latent frame). Tab.~ tab:vdm_prior_compat (a) reports the denoiser's relative reconstruction error at every . Spatial Duplication, the simplest backbone-compatible choice, incurs the largest corrections: constant row-wise tiling is precisely the pattern a video-trained denoiser pushes away from. VAE Encoding fares no better; although designed to pass cleanly through the VAE, it is still treated as off-prior by the denoiser. DCT Encoding instead spreads the signal into smooth cosine bases and sits closest to the prior, attaining the lowest relative reconstruction error at every . What an effective injection must target is compatibility with the denoiser, not merely the encoder a latent passes through. Multi-signal packing. We use the corresponding action chunks, proprioceptive states, and value labels from the same RoboCasa samples to compare four layouts (Fig.~ fig:motivation (d--g)). Separate Spatial Duplication spatially duplicates each signal into its own latent frame, using three frames in total; its reported error is averaged over these frames. Meta-Quadrants puts all three signals into one frame, assigning each an equally sized spatial region and replicating its values along the channel dimension within that region. Meta-Compact also uses one frame and channel-wise replication, but allocates spatial regions according to signal dimensionality: action chunks occupy a larger region, while proprioception and value occupy smaller ones. These two layouts therefore test whether spatial consolidation alone, with either equal or dimension-dependent allocation, is sufficient. Our Unified Meta-Frame instead assigns signals to disjoint channel bands, writes their values into fixed DCT coefficient slots, and applies a per-channel 2D inverse DCT to form one spatial latent. Signals are separated by channel allocation rather than spatial boundaries. Table~ tab:vdm_prior_compat (b) shows that this choice matters beyond frame count. At , Meta-Quadrants and Meta-Compact incur relative reconstruction errors of 0.6730 and 0.6234, respectively, compared with 0.5613 for our Unified Meta-Frame and 0.6178 for Separate Spatial Duplication. title: DroneSegEdit: Adapting Pretrained Generative Editors for UAV Segmentation with Language-Grounded Verification
summary: Recent work has shown that pretrained image generators can support diverse visual tasks. Yet directly applying them to language-guided unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) segmentation exposes a key limitation: a plausible mask may correspond to the wrong instance among small and repeated objects. We call this mismatch between mask rendering and expression-level target selection the Grounding-Rendering Gap. We present DroneSegEdit, which combines RGB proposal rendering with language-grounded, proposal-constrained verification to select supported foreground while retaining rendered geometry. DroneSegEdit adapts the open-weight LongCat-Image-Edit model using task-specific LoRA and fixed color-to-label decoding. For referring segmentation, a Language-Grounded Spatial Verifier (LGSV) reads hierarchical states from the frozen multimodal large language model backbone to derive expression-conditioned spatial evidence, which is mapped back to the rendered proposal without introducing foreground outside it. On RIS-LAD, DroneSegEdit reaches a new state of the art at 52.78 mIoU, 7.16 points above the previous best. It remains competitive overall on UAVid-RIS and VDD-RIS, with its clearest class-wise gains on compact, application-relevant categories, notably vehicles and humans. A separate verifier-free experiment extends the RGB interface to full-scene parsing: a task-specific adapter jointly renders all classes from one task-level instruction without enumerating class names or palette colors.

A referring expression may distinguish the intended instance only through subtle spatial or contextual cues. A successful system must therefore answer two coupled questions: which instance is being referred to, and which pixels belong to that instance. Most referring systems rely on discriminative cross-modal decoders or multimodal reasoning followed by promptable segmentation~ lai2024lisa,chen2024sam4mllm,lv2026resap,kirillov2023sam,nguyen2025vatex,ito2025feature . For UAV perception, this formulation can retain fine spatial structure, produce visually inspectable predictions, and provide a common output space across heterogeneous pixel-level tasks. Its use for language-guided aerial segmentation, however, remains largely unexplored. We adopt the open-weight, instruction-guided ~ longcat2025 . title: A 10K drone image dataset with component-level annotations for rooftop photovoltaic inspection
comment: 14 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary information is included as an ancillary file
summary: Component-level information supports rooftop photovoltaic (PV) inspection, but recognizing individual components across complex scenes remains challenging. We present PVIS-10K, a dataset of 10,065 drone images with component-level annotations covering 63,632 physical PV modules across 22 rooftop installations. The high-resolution red-green-blue (RGB) images were acquired by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs, also known as drones) in Ningbo, Shaoxing and Shenzhen, China. Multi-angle oblique observations capture installation-height and scale variation, dense arrangements, occlusion, shadows and reflections. Three-dimensional delineation, reprojection and image-by-image review produced 3,516,675 image-level polygon annotations, stored in Common Objects in Context (COCO) format. Station-disjoint partitions support evaluation on unseen stations within and across cities. Four supervised models and text-prompted zero-shot Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) provide full-resolution benchmarks of instance matching and foreground coverage. PVIS-10K supports component localization, delineation and image-based counting for drone-based rooftop PV inspection research.

Background Summary sec:background Solar photovoltaic (PV) deployment continues to expand, with distributed rooftop installations forming an important part of this growth pvps2026 . The growing installed asset base increases the need for inspection and maintenance to sustain system performance pvpsom2022 . Component locations, boundaries and arrangement provide a spatial reference for these activities and support image-based counting. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs, also known as drones) provide high-resolution rooftop observations from different viewing angles colomina2014 , supporting component mapping for inspection r4 . PV inventories establish facility locations r1,r2,r3,r13 , while aerial annotations and detection and segmentation studies map array boundaries and PV coverage r7,r11,r12,r8,r9,r10 . title: Obscured Wildfire Flame Detection by Spatio-temporal Analysis of Smoke Patterns Using Frame-wise Transformers
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Published in the 2024 20th International Conference on Distributed Computing in Smart Systems and the Internet of Things (DCOSS-IoT), pp. 58-65
summary: In this paper, we propose a new paradigm in wildfire management for detecting both visible and obscured fire using Deep Learning (DL). The essence of our method is the joint spatial and temporal analysis of RGB videos, embracing the fact that temporal patterns of smoke motions in consecutive video frames can indicate obscured fire flames. This perspective contrasts the traditional approach of independently analyzing images and individual video frames. To this end, we propose a frame-wise transformer architecture that applies an attention mechanism between the consecutive frames while preserving spatial information within frames as opposed to regular attention mechanisms like the non-local block, which combines spatial and temporal information into a single vector. We also optimize the temporal pattern lengths under different spatial resolutions to achieve the highest performance while reducing the computational cost. To investigate the applicability of our method in aerial image processing, we applied it to a curated version of the FLAME2 dataset that includes dual-mode RGB/IR videos. The IR video feed is used to extract ground truth, while the model is trained only on RGB videos to maintain applicability to lowcost commercial drones (which are equipped only with regular cameras) and facilitate processing existing RGB-only datasets. Our proposed method achieves a Segmentation Foreground Dice score of 92.61%, an Object Detection Precision and Recall rate of 93.21% and 91.73%, and clip-level classification accuracy of 98.02%, respectively. We also investigated the efficacy and generalizability of our method through ablation study

Wildfire Monitoring, Obscured Fire Detection, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles, Temporal Video Analysis Introduction Wildfires have become prevalent and destructive in many parts of the world. Regardless of the cause, wildfires can have severe consequences, including the loss of human lives, destruction of property, disruption of wildlife, food production, and crop supply chain as well as significant environmental damage. Once a wildfire starts, there are various ways to monitor and control these wildfires, including observation towers, direct human intervention, satellite imaging, and manned aircraft. Using drones is one of the most efficient ways of fire monitoring due to its low operation cost, customizable sensing and imaging, flexible operation, and ease of use in harsh environments by advanced flight control features and partial autonomy (e.g., safe auto-landing). One of the most significant advantages of using drones in wildfire fighting is the ability of gathering real-time data about the fire’s behavior. Equipped with cameras and other sensors, drones can fly over the fire and capture relevant information. Drones can also be equipped with water tanks or fire extinguishers containing fire-retardant chemicals, such as carbon dioxide (CO2), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3), or evaporating like bromochlorodifluoromethane (CF2ClBr) to be dropped on hot spots to create fire breaks. The efficient utilization of drones will significantly advance controlling these fires. Targeting places where actual burning is happening, instead of blindly spraying fire retardant gases everywhere, will help set these fires off quickly and efficiently. Finding out these burning places in real-time is very difficult, especially when fire flames are obscured by thick smoke. An infrared camera can help find these hidden fires, but IR cameras are expensive when utilized on a large scale. We devised a methodology that uses an RGB camera feed, analyzes the video frames sequentially, and detects the obscured fires using temporal features, such as smoke patterns. We show that such features can be indicative of the fire's exact location and temporal behavior. We formulated the problem as a semantic segmentation of the obscured fire by analyzing the sequence of frames in the video. We propose a deep learning architecture, ‘Frame-Wise Transformer,’ that utilizes a pre-trained CNN backbone to extract the features from video frames and passes through a convolutional transformer that aggregates the video features and sends them to a decoder, which will predict the segmentation map of the fire flames. We have implemented a convolutional transformer mimicking the NLP transformer, treating the video frame features as word embedding. Utilizing the popular non-local block DBLP:journals/corr/abs-1711-07971 for attention mechanism did not yield reasonable results. Therefore, we re-formulated the attention mechanism to restrict attention only between frames while not mixing within the frame information. We modified the non-local block accordingly and achieved a significant performance gain. To balance the spatial resolution and temporal depth, we examined different frame rates while aggregating features at different resolutions. We observed that using more frames at lower resolutions provides higher performance while reducing the computation cost compared to using equal depth at all resolutions. The overall design can be extended to other video-based deep-learning tasks by making minor modifications to accommodate task-specific requirements. To this end, we curated a dataset from the existing FLAME2 shamsoshoara2021aerial dataset by selecting part of video frames from the original data where the drone is stationary, and there is high synchronization with the IR images to avoid misalignment errors. We also use the corresponding IR videos to extract ground truth for our task by performing a series of image-processing operations. We have visually verified the correspondence of RGB video with the processed IR video for frame-level synchronization. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. We highlight the unique features of our method compared to previous methods in Section 2, then proceed by elaborating on the details of the generated dataset and its preparation method in Sections 3 and 4.1. We then elucidate the details of the proposed deep learning (DL) architecture in Section Section 4.2. The obtained results are investigated in Section 5, followed by concluding remarks in Section 6. Related work The previous works on fire detection are mainly based on image-based techniques such as classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation of visible fire imagery. Wonjae Lee et al. proposed a wildfire detection system that classifies the presence of fire in images and evaluated the performance of AlexNet, GoogLeNet, and VGG, along with their modified variants 7889305 . Zhentian et al. have trained YOLOV3 for fire detection and reported a recognition rate of 91 9163816 . An ensemble-based object detection method using YOLOV5 EfficientDet is proposed in xu2021forest for detection and EfficientNet to capture global information about the fire. Their study showed a decrease in false positive rate by 51.3 on public datasets. Yo Zhao et al. have proposed a deep learning architecture, called Fire-Net by stacking convolutional and pooling layers for fast localization and segmentation of fire in aerial images with an accuracy of 98 on standard 'UAV Fire' dataset zhao2018saliency . A similar method is proposed in zhang2022forest and wang2022real by using a deep learning architecture to classify frames into "fire with smoke", "fire with no smoke", and "no fire" using FLAME datasets shamsoshoara2021aerial,swyw-6j78-22 . However, most of these methods are limited to images, whereas real-time data for fire detection will be mostly in terms of video feed. Further, they ignore the fact that video feeds contain temporal patterns of smoke that can help locate the origin of smoke or equivalently the fire spots. Temporal analysis of such patterns, especially in the presence of clouds and other white patterns, can be extremely useful for precise fire detection. This concept is used as a key idea in our method to detect obscured fire positions. Some works take a slightly different approach and analyze fire image patch by patch instead of one-shot analysis of the entire image. For instance, a CNN-based deep learning method is proposed in zhang2016deep which classifies the image first and then performs a patch-level analysis to offer more detailed information. They applied their method to video frames and performed patch-wise detection. They reported a 97 detection accuracy on their own dataset. Still, this method does not consider the temporal relationships for fire classification since it treats the video frame as a sequence of independent still images. In a similar work, Gwangsu Kim et al kim2019fire . proposed an algorithm that collects features of video frames using a pre-trained VGG and stacks them together to be passed through a series of fully connected layers to classify the presence of fire in the video clips. However, this method which restricts fire classification only during a visible fire deemed inefficient in capturing obscured fire. Anshuman et al. dewangan2022figlib have proposed SmokeyNet - a deep learning algorithm that offers stacking CNN, LSTM, and Vision Transformer to detect smoke in the video feed captured by stand-alone cameras. However, this method is not directly applicable to aerial imagery. Some other research works take advantage of Infra-Red (IR) cameras for more accurate fire positioning. For instance, Chi Yuan et al. proposed an algorithm that uses brightness and motion clues with histogram-based segmentation and optical flow to segment fire in IR images yuan2017fire . Another example is Norsuzial et al.'s work that offers an Image processing-based approach to convert IR images to YCbCr color and use a wavelet analyzer to detect fire ya2021image . Also, a DL architecture is proposed in 9953997 that analyzes dual-feed imagery captured by side-by-side RGB and IR cameras for precise fire positioning. Although these methods yield high accuracy taking advantage of thermal information captured by IR cameras, they incur an extra monitoring cost for their reliance on pricey IR cameras. Also, they are not suitable for processing existing drone-based and satellite-based datasets that include only RGB imagery. In contrast to these works, our method uses only RGB videos for detecting both visible and obscured fire flames in an economical way. Data Preparation We investigated different fire datasets and found out that FLAME2 dataset shamsoshoara2021aerial provides the most suitable testing condition because it has videos consisting of visible and obscured fire regions with smoke. Also, it offers a dual mode RGB/IR imagery that simplifies evaluating the proposed framework. FLAME2 consists of seven pairs of lengthy RGB and IR video feeds taken by seven drones equipped with side-by-side RGB/IR cameras. The videos were taken from a prescribed fire region in Kaibab National forest in Northern Arizona. For experimentation purposes, we have carefully cropped the parts of the video where the camera is relatively stationary and there is a high alignment between the RGB and IR camera viewpoints, so IR stands as a legitimate ground truth. The selected video segments are split into clips of 20 consecutive frames to train our deep neural network, where each clip is considered a training sample. In total, we have used 839 video samples for training(594) and evaluating(255) our method. These video samples consist of a diverse set of positive samples consisting of visible and obscured fire regions shot at different locations and negative samples where fire is absent, which are included to make the model robust. title: OnlyAct: Extracting Action Representations from Foundation Models for World Models
summary: Video world models promise general-purpose interactive simulators, but their training is limited by action supervision: action labels are scarce, fragmented across incompatible specifications, and do not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus. A common workaround jointly trains an action encoder to compress consecutive frames into a latent action and a decoder to reconstruct the next frame from the previous frame and that latent, forcing the latent to capture only new information. This has two limitations: learning the action space from scratch can limit generalization to unseen domains, and the bottleneck trades expressiveness for separation, with tighter settings losing nuance and looser ones risking scene leakage under domain shifts. We argue for a different starting point: rather than learning actions from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2), whose embeddings of a frame pair already carry substantial action information after large-scale, diverse video pretraining. The remaining challenge is to extract the action while discarding the scene. We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework that pulls together frame pairs sharing the same motion under a different scene and pushes apart pairs from the same scene with different motion, reshaping the geometry of the pretrained space without imposing a reconstruction bottleneck. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol along three axes (action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality) across robot manipulation, camera navigation, game, and driving benchmarks, most of which are unseen during adaptation. Compared with annotation-free latent-action methods, our representations are substantially more expressive while matching their scene invariance, and they yield world models that transfer demonstrated actions to new scenes more faithfully.

Introduction Over the past few years, video generative models~ brooks2024sora, veo3_2025, HunyuanVideo, wan2025wan have reached unprecedented levels of realism. They are trained on vast quantities of video data and acquire broad priors over scene structure and dynamics, which has motivated their use well beyond video generation itself. A growing line of work explores how they can be turned into video world models by conditioning generation on action signals~ bruce2024genie, parker2024genie2, deepmind2025genie3, gao2025adaworld . Video world models have the potential to serve as general-purpose interactive simulators, with applications ranging from robotics to gaming. Realizing this potential, however, hinges on action supervision. While unlabeled video is abundant, only a small fraction is paired with the actions that produced it, and the labels that do exist are fragmented across incompatible specifications, such as joint angles in robotics or controller inputs in games. Direct action conditioning therefore does not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus and does not transfer well across environments. To overcome this, latent-action models~ menapace2021pvg, bruce2024genie extract latent actions from unlabeled video in a self-supervised manner and use them to condition the video generator during pretraining. Real actions can then be mapped onto this latent space afterward with a small amount of labeled data~ bruce2024genie, gao2025adaworld . Latent-action models are typically trained from scratch as inverse-dynamics models: given a pair of consecutive frames, an action encoder infers a latent intended to capture the action, while a decoder reconstructs the next frame from the previous frame together with this latent. A bottleneck on the latent forces it to encode only what the decoder cannot recover from the previous frame alone, ideally isolating the action signal from scene content. This comes with two limitations: first, training the action space from scratch can prevent it from generalizing to unseen domains; second, tightening the bottleneck improves separation between action and scene at the cost of expressiveness, while loosening it preserves nuance at the cost of scene leakage, which can also hurt generalization when scene, embodiment, or dynamics shift. In this work, we propose , an unlabeled action representation learning framework that takes a different starting point. Rather than learning the action representation from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model, V-JEPA~2~ vjepa2 , and extract actions from it with contrastive learning. Pretrained on large-scale, diverse video, such a model encodes both what is in a scene and how it changes over time, so the action-relevant signal is already present in its embeddings, alongside scene content. We confirm this empirically: when a pair of consecutive frames is encoded as a two-frame clip, even the frozen V-JEPA~2 embedding carries more action information than latent-action models trained on the same data, as measured by a linear probe ( ). However, it also carries more scene information ( ), and its probing performance is unstable across domains. The main challenge is therefore not to learn an action representation from scratch, but to disentangle the action-relevant signal from scene content. We do this by adapting the pretrained foundation model into an action encoder on unlabeled video with a contrastive objective and a lightweight low-rank adapter. Given two frames from a video, we form a positive example that keeps the motion but changes the scene: when the camera is static, we use optical flow to cut out the moving region and paste it, at a shifted location, onto the background of a different scene. Hard negatives are drawn from other frame pairs of the same video, where action provides the dominant axis of variation. Together, these signals shift the encoder embedding space toward action. Crucially, this is achieved without a reconstruction bottleneck: the objective reshapes the geometry of the pretrained space rather than compressing the action into a small code from which the next frame must be decoded. The adapted encoder supports two main uses: transfer from demonstrations, and direct control with real actions. In the first, the encoder extracts a latent action from a pair of demonstration frames; this latent then conditions a video world model to reproduce the same action in a different scene. In the second, a small action-labeled dataset can be used to map an environment's real actions onto the latent space, after which the video world model can be controlled directly through them. Both uses require an action representation that captures rich and discriminative action dynamics, isolates the action signal from scene content so the same action transfers across scenes, and drives faithful action-conditioned video generation across different domains. We construct a unified evaluation protocol around these axes and benchmark against prior annotation-free latent-action methods and the frozen pretrained encoder on thirteen robot, camera-navigation, and game datasets, ten of which are unseen during adaptation, as well as on world-model training and fine-tuning across robot, navigation, game, and driving domains. Our representation is the most expressive on almost all datasets, matches the scene invariance of bottlenecked latent-action models, and yields world models with markedly better action transfer and controllability. Our main contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=2.6em, itemindent=1pt, itemsep=1pt, parsep=2pt, topsep=-2pt] We introduce a new perspective on unlabeled action representation learning: rather than learning actions from scratch, we extract them from the representation space of a pretrained foundation model. We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework, built on flow-guided scene-swapped positives and same-video hard negatives, that disentangles action from scene without a reconstruction bottleneck and improves both action expressiveness and scene invariance over the frozen encoder. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol that systematically probes action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality, and show across robot, navigation, game, and driving benchmarks that our representations improve over prior annotation-free latent-action baselines. Action-conditioned video world models have become a core approach for modeling environment dynamics in domains such as gaming and robotics. Existing methods typically obtain action information in one of two ways. The first assumes explicit action or intervention supervision, such as controller inputs, robot states, camera trajectories, or action prompts~ diamond, unisim, cosmos, gamengen, zhang2025matrixgame, he2025matrixgame2, 2026matrixgame3, huang2025voyager, parker2024genie2, deepmind2025genie3, mao2025yume, Li_2025_ICCV, lingbot-world, xiao2025worldmemlongtermconsistentworld, pondaven2026actionparty . This provides a precise control interface, but the supervision is tied to particular environments, embodiments, or data-collection pipelines, and therefore does not naturally scale to uncurated in-the-wild video. The second introduces latent-action interfaces learned from video~ bruce2024genie, gao2025adaworld, gao2026dreamdojo, lapa, genie_redux, univla , reducing the need for explicit labels but requiring a separate action-learning process. Current interactive video world models therefore face a trade-off between precise but environment-specific action supervision and scalable but separately learned latent actions. Our work is complementary: we use pretrained foundation-model representations as an effective starting point and ask whether they already contain transferable transition structure that can be extracted for world model pretraining. Latent Action Models from Video. A growing line of work learns latent actions from unlabeled video by jointly training an action encoder on frame pairs together with a future-frame decoder, with a bottleneck on the latent. Prior methods reduce this leakage with low-dimensional bottlenecks, discrete codebooks, or other architectural constraints, but these constraints come at the cost of reducing the resolution of the action space.
